articles.title: Who did what? Gracioso details VP Sara, others’ roles in alleged cash delivery scheme
articles.summary: Gracioso, a former police officer who served as the close-in security for former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco from 2017 to 2024, has outlined the specific roles played by Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Dismissed Police Corporal Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. has detailed a highly organized, multi-million-peso cash delivery scheme involving prominent political figures.

Gracioso, a former police officer who served as the close-in security for former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco from 2017 to 2024, has outlined the specific roles played by Vice President Sara Duterte, Velasco and several individuals in moving massive sums of cash across the country.
The testimony of Gracioso is being investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) despite his dismissal from service, according to NBI Director Melvin Matibag.
Both Duterte and Velasco denied the allegations Gracioso made against them.
According to the Bureau of Immigration, Velasco is currently outside the country.
RELATED: Lord Allan Velasco out of Philippines, BI confirms
Sara Duterte’s alleged role
According to Gracioso, Sara Duterte — then the mayor of Davao City — was the primary recipient of the cash deliveries, which were described as her "budget" for allegedly traveling and campaigning.

Gracioso detailed over 10 instances between 2018 and 2020 where he personally delivered suitcases containing between P10 million and P20 million in cash to Duterte upon her arrival by private plane in Pasay, subsequently escorting her to luxury hotels like the Diamond Hotel and Edsa Shangri-La.
The cash deliveries escalated significantly during the 2019 midterm elections and Velasco's speakership, with Duterte allegedly receiving multiple shipments of P50 million to P100 million at a time.
These transactions took place at various locations, including her residence in Davao, the Quezon City Circle and even during a family trip to the Subic Safari. The affidavit reads:

9. Pagdating sa Diamond Hotel inabot ko kay Ma'am Sara ang regalo. Kinuha niya ang paper bag habang inutusan niya ako na ibigay ang maliit na maleta kay Jefry Tupaz ("Jepoy"). Sabi rin niya na sabihin ko kay Ma'am Wen at Boss Allan na "salamat." 10. Ang laman ng inabot kong paper bag ay Royce chocolates na paborito daw ni Ma'am Sara at ang maliit na maleta naman ay naglalaman ng 20M cash. 11. Nasundan pa ito ng humigit sampung beses mula 2018 hanggang 2020. Tuwing dumarating sa Manila si Ma'am Sara sakay ng private plane, susunduin ko siya sa hangar sa Pasay. Pinaabutan siya ni Boss Allan ng pasalubong na Royce Chocolate at maleta na naglalaman ng nasa sampu hanggang dalawampung milyong piso (P10-20 Million) na "budget" niya sa pagiikot. Personal ko itong inaabot kay Ma'am Sara o minsan kapag kasama niya ang katiwala na si Jepoy ay dito niya ito pinaaabot. Inihahatid ko sila sa Diamond Hotel, o kaya naman sa Shangri-la, Edsa.
To maintain distance from the physical cash, Gracioso said that Duterte utilized trusted aides to take custody of the money.
Her primary custodian was Jefry "Jepoy" Tupaz, whom Duterte repeatedly instructed Gracioso to hand the cash-filled suitcases, vehicle keys and cash-laden vans to.

Other aides also stepped in to receive funds; a security detail named “Sir Giroy” accepted two suitcases containing P100 million in Duterte's Davao home, while a staff member named Bryan took delivery of two cash-filled vans at the Diamond Hotel basement.

Furthermore, Duterte introduced Gracioso to Ramil Madriaga, who directly received P20 million in cash for an election caravan and later picked up another P20 million from Velasco's home for a motorcycle riding course in Davao. Gracioso wrote in his affidavit:

23. Kinabukasan, bumalik kami sa bahay ni Ma'am Sara. Doon, ipinakilala sa akin ni Ma'am Sara si Ramil Madriaga ("Sir Ramil") at sinabing sa kanya ko ibigay ang pera pambili ng mga motorsiklong gagamitin sa election caravan ng HNP. Iniabot ko nga ang maleta ng pera na naglalaman ng higit kumulang 20M kay Sir Ramil sa utos ni Ma'am Sara. 24. Noong nabili na ni Sir Ramil ang mga big bike para kay Ma'am Sara, sumama ako kay Ma'am Sara para sa election caravan ng HNP sa Mindanao. Nagikot kami sa ilang mga simbahan at iba pang lugar sa Mindanao para mangampanya para sa mga kandidato ng HNP sa pagka-senador. Pagdating naming sa Cagayan de Oro, doon na ako sumakay ng eroplano pabalik ng Manila.
Velasco’s alleged cash network
According to Gracioso, Velasco served as the coordinator and primary source of the cash delivered to the Vice President.
Gracioso revealed that Velasco accumulated these massive sums from a 25% "all-in" kickback or "SOP" on government projects across the Philippines, which was paid in advance.
Velasco and his wife, Rowena Amara Velasco, initially used their residence at No. 142 Sampaguita St., Valle Verde 2 in Pasig City to count, pack and store the cash.
As the volume of incoming money grew too large to fit in their home, Velasco purchased at least six additional properties in Valle Verde to serve as dedicated "cash houses" or money vaults.

Velasco also personally accompanied some of the cash shipments, even filling his own backpack with money from the suitcases during transit at a private hangar, according to Gracioso. His affidavit states:

16. Sabi ni Ma'am Sara na ibigay kay Jepoy ang dalawang (2) malaking maleta at mga kakanin. Inabot ko yung dalawang malaking maleta na naglalaman ng 50m cash bawat isa at yung mga kakanin kay Jepoy bago sila sumakay ng eroplano. 17. Pagkatapos ng Morion Festival, bumalik kami ni Boss Allan Velasco sa bahay niya sa No. 142 Sampaguita St. Valle Verde 2 para kumuha ng pera at sumunod kami ni Boss Allan sa Davao via isang private Hangar sa Pasay. May dala kaming dalawang (2) malalaking maleta na nasa 100M. Ang pera na ito ay dagdag panggastos ng Hugpong ng Pagbabago (HNP) sa 2019 midterm election. Si Boss Allan, mineet ko na siya sa private Hangar Pasay. Doon pinabuksan niya sa akin yung isang maleta at nagbawas siya ng pera, pinuno niya lang yung backpack niya ng pera galing sa binawas sa isang maleta. 18. Pagdating namin ng Davao, diretso kami sa bahay ni Ma'am Sara. Pag dating sa bahay ni Ma'am Sara Duterte, nag usap si Boss Allan at si Ma'am Sara sa loob ng bahay. Lumabas sila sa bahay at sinabihan ako ni Boss Allan na ibaba na sa sasakyan ang dalawang (2) malaking maleta na naglalaman ng cash. Binitbit ko papunta sa kanila yung dalawang maleta at sinalubong ako nung tao ni Ma'am Sara na si Sir Giroy na security ni Ma'am Sara doon. Kay Sir Giroy ko inabot yung dalawang (2) malaking maleta. Inabot ko naman kay Ma'am Sara ang paper bag na regalo ni Ma'am Wen sa kanya. Doon lang kami sa may receiving area kumain at uminom habang hinihintay si Boss Allan.
Velasco, through his lawyer, denied Gracioso’s claims, saying that his account is “designed and fabricated.”

“The ‘one-size-fits-all’ narrative by this individual seems to be designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events, that is, the Covid-19 pandemic, Atty. Velasco’s period of service as speaker, other details, and even basic common sense,” Velasco’s lawyer, Rowell Ilagan, said.
Paolo Duterte’s alleged involvement
The brother of the Vice President, Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District), also allegedly received money from Gracioso.
In his affidavit, he said that he delivered suitcases of cash to a bar in Davao and other places in Metro Manila. His affidavit states:

44. Nagkaron na din ng pagkakataon na sabay akong nag-deliver ng maleta ng pera sa Davao para kay Ma'am Sara at para kay Cong. Paolo Duterte. 45. Sa utos pa din ni Boss Allan, nag deliver din ako ng maleta ng pera para kay Congressman Paolo Duterte sa isang bar sa Davao at sa iba't-iba pang lugar sa Metro Manila.
As of writing, Philstar.com has sought comment from Duterte’s camp on Gracioso’s allegations. But his camp has yet to reply.
Quimbo, Discayas and Cabral named
Former Rep. Miro Quimbo, according to Gracioso, acted as a key collector of money, which was sourced from the contractor couple Curlee and Sarah Discaya.
According to Gracioso, there were multiple instances where he was ordered by Velasco to pick up cash from Quimbo.
These pickups frequently occurred at a Starbucks in Katipunan — sometimes with the late Public Works and Highways Undersecretary Maria Catalina Cabral in attendance.
Gracioso would then transport the cash back to Velasco's Valle Verde 2 residence, where it was opened and counted by Velasco's personal assistants, Charmaine and Joan. According to his affidavit:

27. Noong naging Speaker na si Boss Allan noong October 2020 ay lalong dumalas at dumami ang mga delivery ng pera sa bahay ni Boss Allan at Ma'am Wen sa Valle Verde 2 galing sa iba't ibang personalidad tulad nila Cong. Zaldy Co, Sir Miro Quimbo, Atty. Honey Sipin.” 28. Kay Sir Miro Quimbo ko rin narinig noong nasa Starbucks Katipunan, malapit sa Miriam College, na galing ang pera kila Curlee Discaya at Sarah Discaya at iba pang DPWH contractor. May isa ring pagkakataon na nakita ko si Eng. Henry Alcantara na papasok sa bahay ni Zaldy Co sa Valle Verde 6 noong pumipick up kami ng pera sa kanya." 29. Sa isang pagkakataon rin, nakita ko si Usec. Maria Catalina Cabral kasama si Sir Miro Quimbo sa Starbucks Petron Katipunan nung utusan ako ni Boss Allan na magpick up ng pera galing kay Sir Miro, na dinala ko naman sa No. 142 Sampaguita St. Valle Verde 2. Binuksan ko ito sa Valle Verde 2 para bilangin at binibigay kay Charmaine at Joan na mga personal assistants o "PA" ni Boss Allan.
As of writing, Philstar.com has sought comment from Quimbo’s camp on Gracioso’s allegations. But his camp has yet to respond.
Zaldy Co’s alleged cash deliveries

According to Gracioso, fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co’s security team frequently delivered cash, which was packed into suitcases and boxes, including balikbayan, Fortune and “Lucky Me” boxes, to the residence of Velasco in Valle Verde.
These deliveries, according to Gracioso, became significantly more frequent and larger in volume after Velasco assumed the speakership in October 2020.

Gracioso personally picked up money from Co at his residence located in Valle Verde 6. During one of these specific cash pickups at Co’s house, Gracioso also witnessed former Bulacan District Engineer Henry Alcantara entering Co’s home.

The connection between their operations was further cemented when Velasco allegedly purchased one of his six "cash houses," which were designated money storage vaults in Valle Verde 6, situated on the exact same street where Zaldy Co’s house was located. Gracioso further stated in his affidavit:

34. Dahil sa dami ng pera na dinedeliver kay Boss Allan ay hindi na kasya ang mga ito sa bahay lamang sa No. 142 Sampaguita Street, Valle Verde 2. Kalaunan, bumili na si Boss Allan ng ilan pang mga bahay sa Valle Verde at sa iba pang mga lugar. Hindi bababa sa anim (6) na bahay ang binili ni Boss Allan sa Valle Verde upang gawing "cash houses" o imbakan ng pera. Isa sa mga cash house na binili ni Boss Allan ay nasa Valle Verde 6, sa parehong kalye kung saan may bahay rin si Zaldy Co. Ilan beses narin akong tumanggap ng pera galing sa kanya na iniimbak namin sa iba't ibang cash houses ni Boss Allan.
Gracioso also received money from Co on multiple occasions to be stored across Velasco's various cash houses.
Additionally, in 2021, Zaldy Co’s security detail arrived at a private hangar in Pasay in a Cadillac and a van to deliver approximately 10 large suitcases of cash.
Co's security loaded these suitcases directly onto a red-and-white private plane, which Gracioso then accompanied to Davao for delivery.

articles.title: Saskatchewan mayor stepping down now that 'Queen of Canada' cult is gone
articles.summary: When Brad Miller signed up to be mayor of Richmound, Sask., he never imagined his tiny southwestern village would be overrun by a cult. After three years and many sleepless nights, the cult is…

image.caption: Richmound, Sask., Mayor Brad Miller says he's stepping down in mid-October after dealing with a cult living in the community during his time in office. (CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan

When Brad Miller signed up to be mayor of Richmound, Sask., he never imagined his tiny southwestern village would be overrun by a cult. After three years and many sleepless nights, the cult is finally gone, and Miller will resign on Oct. 15.
'Nobody knows the hours that I put in,' Richmound's Brad Miller says
When Brad Miller signed up to be the mayor of Richmound, Sask., he never dreamed his tiny southwestern village would be overrun by a cult.
After three years and many sleepless nights, the cult is finally gone.
Miller says he's stepping down on Oct. 15 in hopes that the village can start a new chapter. He is about halfway through a four-year term that was set to end in November 2028.
"We fought a lot of battles and wars, and I think it's just time," he said. "Somebody else can step up and take the reins, and maybe turn a new leaf."
Miller was elected as Richmound's mayor seven years ago. The village of 118 people is roughly 60 kilometres northwest of Maple Creek, near the Alberta border.
"Running for mayor in a small village or town should be a fairly easy thing," he joked.
But for Miller, it was anything but easy. He said he's also dealt with property fraud, disputes over the seniors centre and navigating the financial impact of the pandemic.
"Nobody knows the hours that I put in," Miller said. "It was day after day, week after week, month after month. And I don't think anybody should have to go through that."
Having cult in town like 'living next to dormant volcano,' says Richmound, Sask., resident
Richmound made national headlines on Sept. 15, 2023, when Romana Didulo, the self-proclaimed "Queen of Canada" and her Kingdom of Canada followers moved into an empty school in the village.
She is known as a QAnon conspiracy theorist who started to amass a following during the pandemic.
For two years, the group refused to pay utilities, pumped raw sewage into a children's playground and threatened Miller and others with public executions.
Through it all, Miller was public about how the cult affected his town and continually sought help from the government and RCMP.
"I think Brad needs to be commended for how he handled it, you know, [being] blindsided with this," said Doug Steele, the MLA for Cypress Hills, who represents the area.
"This is a first-time situation, and I think they did quite well. It was pretty stressful for that community."
The RCMP raided the school on Sept. 3, 2025, arresting and removing members of the cult after receiving a report one of its occupants had a gun.
The Saskatchewan Health Authority declared the building "unfit for human habitation" and issued a public health order forcing the eviction of its occupants.
Sask. village mayor upset Crown stayed charges against cult leader
Didulo was charged with failing to comply with an undertaking and intimidating a justice system participant. The Crown stayed her charges last March.
Miller said he's very disappointed in the justice system for that decision.
'A bright future'
Since the cult was pushed out, things are relatively back to normal in the village.
"Well, for the village of Richmound, I feel great that we finally won the war," Miller said. "And I think there's a bright future."
Scott Earl and his wife, Mel, are among those helping the community start over.
The couple moved to town a week before the cult did.
"We like to watch a lot of those documentaries about cults," Scott Earl joked. "Never thought [I'd] live through one."
Earl said it wasn't the fresh start he was expecting, but he's excited to be a part of a new future for Richmound.
"Everybody's bringing in new ideas to build the community, and I think we need to focus on those things rather than always looking in the rearview mirror."
He's the project co-ordinator for Grow Together, an initiative to build an all-seasons domed greenhouse.

"The idea behind the project is to have the villagers initiate some action by coming into the greenhouse, volunteering their time to either weed, plant, water," Earl said. "And by doing that, they'll be able to take a harvest from the greenhouse as well."
Richmound has a corner store, but the nearest grocery store with fresh produce is a 50-minute drive away.
"This is to try and help with food insecurity that we're battling across Canada right now, and to give rural Saskatchewan an advantage on being able to sustain ourselves," Earl said.
Grow Together plans to dehydrate any leftover food to create dry soups or food packs that can be donated to other food banks in the area.
The project got started using a $10,000 grant to address food insecurity. Fundraising initiatives continue, and Earl said they're only at two-thirds of the current fundraising goal.
The group is placing an order for the structure this month and is hoping the greenhouse can be up and operating by July.
Earl said he's sad Miller won't be marking the greenhouse's opening as mayor.
"He was an ambassador for the town — always friendly, engaging, willing to put the best efforts for the village forward," he said.
"It's kind of sad to see Brad step down because after going through all that, I think he should have had at least a few years of down time, where things are going in the right direction."
Miller is planning on staying in Richmound, where he lives with his wife. He said he's looking forward to watching the future community growth from the sidelines.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Halyna Mihalik is a journalist and weather specialist for CBC Saskatchewan. She holds a degree in journalism from the University of Regina. Halyna enjoys stories about advocacy, local politics and rural communities. Send Halyna news tips at halyna.mihalik@cbc.ca
- With files from Colleen Silverthorn

articles.title: Gaza: NGO reports dire camp conditions, says Israel is moving 'Yellow Line'
articles.summary: The Danish Refugee Council alleges that Israel is employing "a policy of protracted displacement" in Gaza. It says the so-called "Yellow Line" is creeping west toward the coast, preventing many from…

image.caption: With much of Gaza either severely damaged or behind Israel's 'Yellow Line,' more than 80% of residents are estimated to be living in makeshift displacement campsImage: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS

blocks.text: A new report on conditions in the Gaza Strip says that the roughly 1.8 million Palestinians in Gaza, or 86% of the population, living in displacement sites often face inhumane living conditions.

The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) published its findings on Thursday, almost three years after the October 7 terror attacks against Israel that triggered the war in Gaza, and a year after the phased October 10 ceasefire plan that was supposed to usher in the war's end.

"The October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza was supposed to end civilians' suffering. Nearly a year on, it exists largely in name only. Displacement in Gaza has not ended; it has changed shape," the report says.
The findings are based on group discussions with 195 people living in internal displacement camps across five governorates in Gaza.
What did the DRC say about the Yellow Line?
Entitled "Confined by Design: The Human Cost of Protracted Displacement in Gaza," the report accuses Israel of "a policy of protracted displacement" since the ceasefire deal was reached.

One means of ensuring this, the DRC says, is the so-called "Yellow Line," which demarcates the area of eastern Gaza near the border that is controlled by the Israeli military and is, according to the report, creeping toward the coast.

"In addition to protracted displacement for hundreds of thousands of people, the defining feature of the so-called ceasefire is the Yellow Line which continues expanding westward and swallowing up more land, effectively squeezing families into 30% of Gaza's territory," said the NGO's country director for the occupied Palestinian territories, Alan Moseley.

blocks.caption: The 'Yellow Line' devides Gaza into two sectionsImage: Omar Ashtawy/APAimages/IMAGO

blocks.text: Other groups, including the UN, have also reported the westward movement of the Yellow Line, as has the Israeli government, although some details differ.
Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put the share of Gaza's territory inside the Yellow Line at 60% rather than 70%, but he also said the plan was to expand the area.
The DRC report also said aid organizations "describe being unable to operate within several kilometers of the line, either due to access constraints or security concerns."
It said that this led to crucial aid and supplies failing to reach displacement camps nearer the boundary.
What did the report say about living conditions in displacement camps?

The DRC and the Agricultural Development Association (PARC) highlighted a series of major shortcomings in the often informal tent shelters and makeshift camps that have sprung up amid Gaza's rubble, where more than eight in 10 residents are believed to be living.
These included but were not limited to:

items: 80% of respondents reporting shortages of water both for washing and drinking
Displaced households relying on outdoor cesspits
Multiple families sharing single latrines, increasing the risk of gender-based violence and abuse
Rat and rodent infestations exacerbated by the unsanitary conditions
Food scarcity and lacking infrastructure for cooking, increasing risks of burns or injury preparing meals
Rapid localized spread of illnesses and infections. For instance, more than 4,000 chickenpox cases were recorded in Khan Younis displacement camps in July alone
Lacking and overburdened medical facilities with only half of hospitals and just over a third of primary healthcare centers still operational
Lacking or non-existent formal education provision for young people, now lasting almost three years in some cases
Reports of security concerns, particularly among men, because of the continued presence of artillery strikes, drones and stray gunfire
Safety risks posed by unexploded and undiscovered ordnance, particularly when trying to clear rubble or return to areas where people originally lived

blocks.caption: The report warned of growing risks of domestic violence, citing both limited and shared facilities, and deteriorating mental health of adult males in the circumstances Image: Mohammad Kuhil/Danish Refugee Council

blocks.text: The Danish Refugee Council also laid particular emphasis on lacking site management mechanisms at displacement camps.
It said only 36% of sites currently had a designated site manager, typically a national NGO, coordinating services and managing conditions.

Sites with such partners "have a structured community channel through which a gap, such as a collapsing cesspit, a missing water delivery, or an unsafe walkway, can be identified, escalated, and resolved," the report said.
Israel has not yet commented on the newly released report.
What actions did the DRC recommend?

The DRC and PARC issued a number of appeals and recommendations, some to "all parties to the conflict," most to "the Government of Israel, as the occupying power of Gaza" and others to "the international community" and "donors and humanitarian actors."
These included:

items: Completely upholding pledges to cease hostilities
Ending attacks against civilians, humanitarian workers and medical personnel
Guaranteeing humanitarian access and medical evacuation pathways
Supporting the establishment of a UN mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations.

blocks.text: The groups called on Israel to "halt the further expansion of the Yellow Line" and to "disclose its current and future route transparently."
They also urged Israel to cease the construction of permanent military infrastructure in the area and to provide "credible assurance that current troop positions are not intended to be permanent."

They appealed for fewer restrictions on aid access, particularly so-called "dual-use" restrictions affecting medical supplies, water, sanitation and hygiene items, pest control, rubble removal and fuel.
The report also warned that political and donor interest in the situation had declined markedly in the year since the ceasefire, even though conditions had not improved proportionately.
UN report condemns Israeli military action in Gaza

articles.title: Trekkers helicoptered off mountains as more deadly landslides hit Nepal
articles.summary: A month after mass catastrophic flooding, around 30 people have died in landslides and heavy rain.

blocks.text: Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal during floods
ByNavin Singh Khadka
Environment correspondent, BBC World Service
Another wave of landslides and heavy rain have killed about 30 people in Nepal, as the Himalayan nation reels from August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands more missing.
The national disaster management authority says more than 1,900 families have been affected since late last week with more than 240 homes damaged. Roads, buildings and bridges have been swept away.
Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit - crucial to Nepal's economy - have had to cut short their hikes to get to safety.
Many have been helicoptered out of the districts of Manang and Mustang, from a hiking circuit that usually takes up to three weeks to complete.
Communities in several parts of Nepal are mourning loved ones.
Speaking from a damp, blue tent in Battar, a town north-west of Kathmandu, Buti Tamang told BBC Nepali: "We used to live in a hut, but now there is nothing. We have lost so many of our relatives."
"Now it is raining and the tent leaks, so we've been facing a difficult situation. We have nowhere to go," said Ramesh Ghale, who also had to flee his home.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many Nepalis have been made homeless and are staying in emergency tents, as a new wave of extreme weather strikes

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Many Nepalis have been made homeless and are staying in emergency tents, as a new wave of extreme weather strikes
Several trekkers and their guides say their journeys back down the mountains have been treacherous, taking up to three or four days and requiring them to pass collapsed roads and swept-away bridges.

Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, found himself stranded with his guide in Yak Kharka, upper Manang, due to heavy snowfall last week and decided not to continue to the Thorang La pass, the highest point of the circuit.

"We made our own paths on mountain slopes," he said, after returning to base camp in Pokhara on Tuesday night. "It was quite steep and we were clambering because there was river below… It was very muddy and very wet.
"Many trekkers were helicoptered out," he added.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jake Stacy and his guide had to craft their own paths on the mountains to return after heavy snowfall

blocks.text: Image source, Jake Stacy
Jake Stacy and his guide had to craft their own paths on the mountains to return after heavy snowfall

Australian Andrew Graham and his guide Prem KC said they had to cross more than 15 landslides after they decided to return from Manang village. "A few of them were quite dangerous, the residual risks have grown now."
The two got stuck when they reached the village of Chame, which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides, and had to spend a night in the jungle, Graham said.

A massive landslide has partially blocked a river which passes through Chame, causing a temporary lake that has inundated houses and a key bridge. Authorities have been trying to release the water for the past three days using excavators but have not been very successful, locals told the BBC.

Meanwhile, trekking guide Tse Ring Doma said she and her group had to cross 28 landslides. The mental stress was more difficult than the physical challenge, she said, given the fresh memory of last month's enormous disaster: "Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way."

Her client, Norwegian Ellen Wahlström, said visitors were fortunate - they would only have to leave some of their items behind, while locals risked losing their houses and land. She added that authorities had been clearing many of the landslides "surprisingly fast".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trekkers have faced difficulties trudging across the landslide-ravaged landscape - and around 700 have been prevented from even starting the Annapurna Circuit

blocks.text: Trekkers have faced difficulties trudging across the landslide-ravaged landscape - and around 700 have been prevented from even starting the Annapurna Circuit

While road damage in Manang has been serious, with several bridges swept away and communications down in some areas, no one had been killed in the trekking region, chief district officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said.
But four bodies have been recovered and 12 people remain missing after an avalanche near the base of Himlung Peak, close to the border with Tibet.
A representative of the local trekking authority, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said some 700 trekkers were still waiting in Pokhara to embark on the Annapurna Circuit.
"We have been holding back all these people who want to go to the Annapurna Circuit trek, although we are under pressure from the trekking industry to announce the route open," he said.
Indian visitors who often visit the ancient temple Muktinath on a Hindu pilgrimage had been asked to fly from Jomson to Pokhara instead of drive down, due to a cut-off road, he added.

blocks.caption: A basic map showing the districts of Mustang and Manang, and how the Annapurna Circuit weaves its way through both of them.

blocks.text: Most of the old trekking trails on the Annapurna Circuit have been unused in recent years after the introduction of roads, except for small pockets of Manang and Mustang districts.
But now operators say many trekkers have been using these abandoned paths to return, as the main roads have been washed away in some sections of the circuit.
Additional reporting by BBC Nepali

articles.title: The NHL final is no longer free to watch. This group wants to pass a law to change that
articles.summary: Next year, for the first time in decades, Canadians won't be able to watch the NHL Stanley Cup final for free on television. A lobby organization wants the government to pass a law to prevent that…

image.caption: The Edmonton Oilers play against the Vancouver Canucks at Rogers Place in Edmonton on Wednesday. Since CBC stopped airing NHL games on Hockey Night in Canada, Canadians who want to watch must do so on cable or subscription streaming channels. (Leila Devlin/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

Next year, for the first time in decades, Canadians won't be able to watch the NHL Stanley Cup final for free on television. A lobby organization wants the government to pass a law to prevent that from happening.
Sports events tied to 'shared national identity' shouldn't be behind paywalls: Friends of Canadian Media
Next year, for the first time in decades, Canadians won't be able to watch the NHL Stanley Cup final for free on television — unless a media lobby group gets its way.

Friends of Canadian Media is asking the federal government to enact legislation that would compel private media companies to license sports events of national importance to TV stations that will air them free of charge.

"We're suggesting that the government ask a simple question: Are there certain moments that are so important to Canada's cultural life that every Canadian should have affordable and broad access to them?" Raj Shoan, the group's executive director, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
"Quite often, a shared national identity is tied to sporting events."
CBC has reached out to the Department of Canadian Heritage for comment.
LISTEN | Interview with Friends of Canadian Media's Raj Shoan:
As It Happens6:33Canada should pass law to make NHL finals free to watch, says media lobby group
Shoan says the campaign is a direct response to news that NHL games are no longer airing on CBC, Canada's public broadcaster.

CBC and Rogers Sportsnet, the national rights holder of Hockey Night in Canada, announced in July that they weren't able to reach a new sublicensing deal that would have allowed CBC to air the program.
CBC recently announced it will bring back Hockey Night by airing
on Saturday nights starting in December. But as it stands, NHL games are only available on cable channels or streaming platforms Sportsnet+ and Amazon Prime.
Prime Video to exclusively stream Wednesday NHL games in Canada
Shortly after the CBC-Rogers deal broke down, Sportsnet announced it's raising the cost of its annual premium subscription by $20.

"When we looked at that in totality we thought, wow, that's really problematic and worrisome because the end result of all of that is higher cost for Canadians and less universal access to a shared national experience that sports often provide," Shoan said.
What is 'anti-siphoning' legislation?
Friends of Canadian Media is asking supporters to contact their members of Parliament and ask them to support what's known as "anti-siphoning legislation" in Canada.

Already in place in several European and Commonwealth countries, Shoan says anti-syphoning laws are designed to prevent private companies from "siphoning off the most valuable programming … and putting them up behind paywalls."

In the U.K., for example, broadcasting regular Ofcom maintains a list of events of national importance that includes the Olympics, the FIFA World Cup and the Rugby World Cup, among others. Rights holders for those events are required to license them to free-to-air broadcasters at "fair and reasonable" prices.
Australia, Ireland and several European Union member states maintain similar lists.

"We're not saying that Rogers doesn't have the right to negotiate these deals. They absolutely do. But what we're saying is, certain programming carries public value in addition to commercial value," Shoan said.
"They can continue to sub-licence it out to whoever they want to under the auspices of this policy."

items: Local hockey fans adjust to watching NHL games without Hockey Night in Canada on CBC
A new NHL season starts today — here's a catch-up on Canada's teams

blocks.text: CBC reached out to Rogers Sportsnet to ask whether it would support anti-siphoning legislation or consider offering certain sports events for free.

"Sportsnet is focused on delivering more NHL content, including more national games with fewer blackouts, to more Canadians across multiple platforms and investing in bringing world-class hockey coverage to Canadian fans," the company said in an emailed statement.
The NHL did not respond CBC's request for comment before deadline, but spokesperson Jon Weinstein told the Globe and Mail it is "committed to more games in more places than ever before."
'It's your time and your money'
Already, Canadians are feeling the impact of the NHL rights change on their wallets, reports CBC Edmonton, which spoke to Edmonton Oilers fans and the owners of businesses that air Oilers games.

"Now to get something, you're going to have to give up something," Moshe Lander, a sports economist at Concordia University in Montreal, said. "Up until this past year, if you wanted to watch, the only thing you really had to give up was your time. Now, it's your time and your money."
How will hockey fans navigate an NHL season without CBC’s Hockey Night in Canada?
While the Friends of Canadian Media campaign is focused on the Stanley Cup final, Shoan says Canada's list could include other sporting events, too.

He wants the government to direct Canada's broadcasting regulator, the CRTC, to explore what anti-siphoning legislation could look like in Canada, and consult with the public about what events should be included.

"Canadians have embraced streaming, and that's not going to change. But for us, it's really an issue of shared cultural experiences," Shoan said. "We think there's a public interest conversation that needs to be had."
With files from Nicholas Frew and Tristan Mottershead. Interview with Raj Shoan produced by Lara Hindle

articles.title: Canadian websites take down articles written by suspected fake, AI-generated persona
articles.summary: Several Canadian websites have taken down articles published under the name Daniel Robson, saying the writer's identity cannot be verified and was likely generated by AI.

image.caption: Several Canadian websites and news outlets, including the Ottawa Citizen, Montreal Gazette and Policy Options, removed articles written by someone using the name Daniel Robson after questions began to mount over their identity. (Wilfredo Lee/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Several Canadian websites have taken down articles published under the name Daniel Robson, saying the writer's identity cannot be verified and was likely generated by AI.
Several Canadian websites say writer's persona cannot be verified, was likely generated by AI
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 5:29 PM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

Who is Daniel Robson? That's the question editors, journalists and other observers are asking after several Canadian websites took down articles written by someone using that name — but whose identity they now say cannot be verified and was likely generated by artificial intelligence.

The digital magazine Policy Options said last week that it removed an article published last year under Robson's name after it was "unable to independently establish that the person who wrote for us is who he represents himself to be or that the biographical information he provided is accurate."

On Tuesday, the Ottawa Citizen also said opinion columns written by Robson, who was published three times in the newspaper last year, were taken down after an investigation uncovered that he "does not seem to be a real person."

items: ‘It’s really disturbing’: Yukoners say AI-generated website dangerous

blocks.text: The announcements came after an editor at Turkiye Today contacted Canadian editors with questions about Robson's identity after Robson approached the Turkey-based news outlet with a story about a purported drug plot involving people in Turkey and Canada.
So what happened, and what do we know about the Robson persona?
Self-described 'terrorism and crime' expert

Les Perreaux, editor in chief of Policy Options, wrote in a statement on Sept. 24 that the magazine published a piece under Robson's name last year after he had introduced himself as "an independent Canadian journalist from Montreal."
Robson had been published by other Canadian media and he was co-operative through several rounds of editing, Perreaux told CBC News on Wednesday.
But when he was contacted by the editor in Turkey and started to investigate, Perreaux said he couldn't confirm Robson's identity. He acknowledged the vetting process didn't go far enough.

"Publication history and personal contact aren't enough anymore," Perreaux said. "You have to go further to find the breadcrumbs that can reassure you that the person is real, and that they have the expertise they claim."

Ottawa Citizen editor in chief Nicole Feriancek also said in a written statement on Tuesday that Robson had described himself as a "'Canadian journalist' specializing in extremism, terrorism and crime."

A "Daniel Robson" profile on X, which uses the same image Robson used on author pages on other websites, describes the writer as an "independent journalist" focused on "extremism, terrorism & cybercrime."
But Feriancek said Robson's "headshot, based on online analysis tools, appeared to be AI generated, as did the writing he submitted."
CBC News also put the image used on Robson's X page through an AI analysis tool, which said it was likely created by AI.
Feriancek said attempts to call or meet Robson were rebuffed.
"When we were up front with our concerns, and said we wanted to verify his identity — in person — he declared he was incensed by our line of questions, and he ended all communication."
Fake journalists, real harm: this AI website is claiming to cover northern news
Where else did Robson write?

Robson — who largely wrote about domestic issues in Canada, such as hate-crime legislation and national security — had author pages at the Hub, Open Canada and Western Standard. As of Wednesday, they had all been taken down.

"Daniel Robson's columns were removed from the Western Standard website after multiple media organizations investigated his background, and he was unable to verify his identity," reads a note on the Western Standard website.

items: Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?

blocks.text: An article was also published under Robson's name in the Montreal Gazette, which on Wednesday afternoon said the piece had been retracted.

"Following this incident, we have strengthened our contributor verification procedures and implemented additional checks to safeguard against [these] new forms of fraud," editor in chief Lenie Lucci wrote.
What set off the investigation into Robson's identity?

In an article published on Tuesday, Turkiye Today's managing editor Ilker Sezer said the outlet received an email in early September from Robson, pitching a story about a drug ring purportedly involving a Moroccan-Canadian businessman who is an outspoken critic of Morocco.

"I like such stories, like crime thrillers, so I was kind of excited: 'Oh, Moroccan drug lord laundering money through a Turkish middleman? Wow, yeah,'" Sezer recalled thinking. "He had this sense of urgency; he wants to get [the story] out ASAP."
But Sezer told CBC News on Wednesday that when he began digging into the allegations from Istanbul and asked Robson for more information, alarm bells began to ring.
"I offered a video call with him just to discuss the details of the case and he refused. This was the first moment that I got [suspicious]."
A review of his emails from Robson, as well as work published on other websites under that name, then made Sezer think the person was using AI.

According to Sezer, when Robson became aware that he was asking questions, he became agitated. In Robson's last email to him, about two weeks ago, "he said there will be repercussions for what you have done to me," Sezer said.
Who's behind the Robson persona?
Sezer said he can't say for sure, but he thinks there is a link to Morocco.

In his Turkiye Today piece, Sezer wrote that Robson's work "revealed a coordinated agenda: fiercely defending the Moroccan state while orchestrating targeted information campaigns against its critics."
CBC News could not independently verify such a link. CBC News also was not able to reach Robson via email on Wednesday afternoon.

The Globe and Mail reported on Wednesday that a digital research tool showed that Robson's email address was used to register a Moroccan Microsoft account in March. "That account was last active in early September, records show," it said.

Whoever is behind it, Sezer said the episode underscores that journalism is in "a period of transition" as the use of AI expands globally. "Being cognizant of AI and its dangers is very important right now."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: Telcos ready temporary disaster roaming before summer

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor

Telstra, Optus and Vodafone will from today be able to move users over to one of their rivals’ networks in areas where coverage has dropped out due to natural disasters such as cyclones, bushfires or floods.
The capability will mean users in those areas will still be able to call, message, and get basic access to the internet if the other network is up at no additional cost.
This is beyond the existing capability for networks to hand over emergency triple zero calls to other networks when the call can’t get through.
The industry has flagged there will be some scenarios - such as power outages – when switching will not be possible.
The switch-on for temporary roaming will be managed by the three carriers, and will happen automatically for customers when activated.

The temporary disaster roaming can be activated in up to three affected areas at the same time, with up to 15 mobile sites included per area, and activated for 24 hours at a time. The disaster areas must be at least 400km apart.
Metropolitan areas are excluded from the roaming arrangement.
Good morning, Nick Visser here to pick up the blog. Let’s get into Thursday.

blocks.caption: Henry Belot

blocks.text: Henry Belot

From today, children under nine years old with mild developmental delays and autism can access early intervention services through a program called Thriving Kids, which is administered by state and territory governments.

The change was announced by the Albanese government in August 2025 and will slowly move children off the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It will fully replace the NDIS for these children by 2028.
Unlike the NDIS, participation in Thriving Kids won’t require a formal diagnosis, potentially speeding up services and saving families money.
The health minister, Mark Butler, recently told parents there would be no gap in government support for their children.
Queensland is the sole Australian state refusing to sign on to the Thriving Kids program, leaving families in limbo as the first phase of the NDIS replacement scheme launches.
You can read more details about the change here:
ATO finds one-quarter of big firms pay zero tax

blocks.caption: Jonathan Barrett

blocks.text: Jonathan Barrett
More than one-quarter of big companies operating in Australia paid no income tax in 2024-25, according to the Australian Taxation Office’s latest corporate transparency report.
The report says companies mostly cited an accounting loss – when expenses outstrip revenue.

Guardian Australia has previously reported how some multinationals, including the Singtel-owned Optus and coal miner Adani, regularly pay no tax, citing infrastructure investments and operating expenses .
About 27% of entities in the report reported zero tax, which was a similar figure to the year before.
In total, 4,299 entities earning at least $100m in total income paid a combined $87.5bn in tax in 2024–25, led by Australia’s large mining sector.
The ATO acting deputy commissioner, Michelle Sams, says the agency is “increasingly focused” on making sure digital businesses and supply chains, including data centres, paid their share of tax.

double quotation markWe look very closely if there’s no tax being paid in significant industries, including things like data centres, to make sure that the level of tax being paid reflects the economic activity that’s happening in Australia.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Human rights panel condemns Canada's inaction regarding Indigenous people
articles.summary: Canada is failing to meet international legal obligations by refusing to hold thorough investigations into the crimes committed in its residential school system, says a global human rights…

image.caption: The Permanent Peoples' Tribunal judges, from left to right, Seanna Howard, Frances Webber and Valmaine Toki give preliminary conclusions following a week of hearings in Montreal in May. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Canada is failing to meet international legal obligations by refusing to hold thorough investigations into the crimes committed in its residential school system, says a global human rights organization.
Final report released to coincide with National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 5:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago
The Permanent Peoples' Tribunal issued its final report Wednesday, saying that the residential schools posed "widespread, systematic and most serious human rights violations."

Released to coincide with the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the 78-page report urged Canada to investigate, prosecute and punish the perpetrators of these violations, and to provide reparations. The tribunal accused the country of doing "very little" to prevent the continuation of discrimination against Indigenous Peoples.

The judgment also condemned Canada for showing "deliberate … contempt" before the international community. It said the country refused to sign certain international conventions and modify its criminal law to include genocide, enforced disappearances and apartheid.
Recognition 'mostly deprived of practical effect'
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and the House of Commons recognized in 2019 and 2022 that the operation of the residential school system constituted an act of genocide.
However, the tribunal's report called the acknowledgments "mostly deprived of practical effect by the extremely limited criminalization of genocide in Canadian domestic legislation.”

It also said those recognitions "have not had tangible consequences or been accompanied by any substantial change in the public policies of the successive governments regarding the treatment of Indigenous Peoples."

The tribunal reviewed extensive evidence gathered during its hearings last May. The evidence showed that some 15,000 Indigenous children were taken from their communities and sent to residential schools where they were forbidden to speak their language.
The children then faced poor living conditions, inadequate or nonexistent health care, malnutrition, forced labour, harsh discipline and punishment, and sexual abuse.
Continued discrimination, report says

Indigenous people face continued discrimination, namely through the forced and coerced sterilization of women as well as the removal of children from their communities by welfare services fuelled by a lack of support for Indigenous children both on and off reserves, said the report.

Drawing on the definitions in the International Convention on Genocide, the tribunal concluded that Canada failed to end and remedy the acts of genocide. It cited the Canadian government's refusal to fund and support the search for missing Indigenous children and their graves.
The judgment additionally accused Canada of "ongoing land theft and the criminalization of Indigenous land defenders by police and other government agencies."

The actions taken by Canada, the report states, amount to crimes against humanity, as defined by international conventions. These include the enslavement of children through forced labour, the forced transfer of population, severe deprivation of physical liberty, rape and other forms of sexual violence of comparable severity, forced sterilization, and persecution on racial grounds.
Apartheid system in place

It also concluded that Canada had a system of apartheid in place. The report defines apartheid as the institutionalization of segregation and discrimination against a subjugated racial group by a dominant racial group.

In its recommendations, the tribunal asked Canada to conduct thorough investigations into the disappearance and deaths of children in its institutions and that residential schools' archives and records be conserved.

items: Canada continuing genocide against Indigenous Peoples, international tribunal finds

blocks.text: It called on the government to provide financial support for research related to residential school burial sites, to commemorate and protect these sites, and to fund the revitalization of Indigenous languages.
All sacred objects held by governments, museums, national parks, and academic institutions should be returned to the communities to which they belong, it added.

Several recommendations focus on improving conditions on reserves, particularly in the areas of health and education. Others address respect for territorial rights and reparations for land dispossession.

Other recommendations target the Catholic Church and other religious communities who operated the residential schools, including reparations for stolen land and the restitution of these lands where former churches are located.

articles.title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
articles.summary: Other passengers on the Israel-bound flight described the "terrifying" moment the plane dropped.

blocks.text: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.
Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped.
The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes.
"Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.
He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.

When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane".
"I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said.

"We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."
The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.
They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
"Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".
Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment".
"Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.
A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane".
The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".
The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.

articles.title: Pentagon confirms U.S. military will cut 20% of generals and admirals
articles.summary: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. military will cut 20 per cent of its generals and admirals as he made a series of announcements in what he called his "state of the…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirmed more cuts to admirals and generals of the U.S. armed forces during a speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico Wednesday. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. military will cut 20 per cent of its generals and admirals as he made a series of announcements in what he called his "state of the force" address.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth called the cuts 'accountability and long overdue'

Hegseth was speaking to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row that he has given such an address. This time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide.
The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth's predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings.

The Pentagon chief, however, again led with how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls "woke" culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for "testosterone deficiency" among male personnel.

Pentagon officials had previewed that Hegseth would announce more cuts to the number of generals and admirals. He directed all military services to double the 10 per cent reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a total 20 per cent decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
"I call it accountability and long overdue," he said.
New drone-focused warfare command

The Pentagon chief announced the creation of a new four-star command to oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities in what he called "the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history."

The rollout comes a month after officials said an army unit based in Europe that specialized in drone warfare had been directed to return to being a traditional infantry battalion, ending its efforts to learn and use the battlefield technology.

A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers subsequently asked the army to explain the order, given that the world's battlefields are rapidly evolving and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight.

items: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report
Pentagon makes testosterone screening mandatory for U.S. service members effective immediately

blocks.text: The announcement of the new drone command comes with the U.S. in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy shipping corridor. The war has forced U.S. forces in the region to expend hundreds of expensive missile interceptors to defend against Iran's missile and drone attacks, which have still managed to kill and wound U.S. troops.

Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has destroyed Iran's navy, air force and defence systems as well as many of its leaders and its industrial base. But the Islamic Republic has continued intermittently to launch drone and missile attacks against U.S. or allied bases in the region, while maintaining its ability to strike commercial and military ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

During his speech, Hegseth touted the Trump administration's major investments in the defence industry and push for contractors to speed up their work to expand the nation's weapons arsenals. But experts say U.S. military contractors will need at least three years to replenish stockpiles of key weapons systems used heavily in the Iran war.
Criticism over cuts to general ranks

Members of Congress have criticized the war and the drawdown of munitions stockpiles, and some called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" of the military's top ranks that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," said Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot and NASA astronaut, who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning behind the decision.
"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.

items: Trump's army secretary becomes latest military leader to quit administration
Hegseth pushes back on reports of poor conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln in Middle East

blocks.text: Trump or Hegseth already have fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office, including the U.S. army's top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George, a move that angered both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. The departures also have included a number of senior officers who are women or people of colour.

articles.title: 'A trip down memory lane': N.S. man reunited with wallet lost 51 years ago
articles.summary: Carpenter Matty Goldsmith discovered a wallet last week in Dartmouth N.S., returning a time capsule of 1970 memories to its long-lost owner.

image.caption: Richard Gilroy was excited to reclaim his wallet lost in 1975, with everything in it fully intact. (Submitted by Donna Gilroy)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Carpenter Matty Goldsmith discovered a wallet last week in Dartmouth N.S., returning a time capsule of 1970 memories to its long-lost owner.
Social media successfully brought about a lost-and-found reunion spanning half a century
An accidental discovery at a house renovation site in Dartmouth, N.S., and a social media post have reunited a wallet lost 51 years ago with its owner.

While renovating a house for his company on Victoria Road, carpenter Matty Goldsmith found a wallet under the old floors containing identification documents including a driver's licence and student ID, as well as a 1975 theatre ticket for Hamlet and a dollar bill.
Goldsmith and his colleagues were surprised that everything was fully intact, and they guessed that the owner was a high school student who used to work there as a construction labourer.
"I decided like, why not try our luck with the internet and see if we can track this person down," he said.
His post quickly drew responses from the community, including owner Richard Gilroy's wife. Three days later, they met up and returned the wallet to Gilroy.
"I was very surprised to say the least," 68-year-old Gilroy told CBC News on Wednesday. "I'm very pleased to get it all back."
Although Gilroy remembers when and where he lost the wallet, his memory of what's inside has faded.
"It's very interesting that my original handwritten birth certificate was in my wallet, and I have no idea why my parents would have even given it to me,” Gilroy said.
As for the Hamlet ticket, he had no recollection of having seen the play, but said the $1.50 ticket price is "amazing."
Gilroy said he's thankful for Goldsmith, and he's planning to frame everything in his wallet to put on display.
Time capsules
Goldsmith said his job often brings him "little treasures and time capsules."
He once found some letters written in Chinese in a Vancouver renovation site, and a bottle of cobra whisky.
But this is the first time he uncovered someone's ID. Goldsmith said he quickly realized it's a long-lost item.
"It's always neat to think about like who left this here or what their life was like," he said.
He said it was pleasant to meet with Gilroy and his wife, and Gilroy was excited to "have that little piece of his past back in his hands."
"He was able to have a bit of this luck and get this time capsule," Goldsmith said. "It was such a nice trip down memory lane for him."

articles.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
articles.summary: Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are moving forward with plans to establish deportation centers outside the EU. An African partner country has reportedly already been selected.

image.caption: Prospective migrants who arrived in Greece are taken into a migration hubImage: Sofia Kleftaki/DW

blocks.text: Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles.

During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called "return hubs" is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency.

Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda, but neither country has been confirmed as the location.
No sealed detention centers
"We are not talking about centers in the sense that someone whose asylum application is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country," Plevris said.
The plan was rather to establish "open facilities" while the final return to the actual country of origin is being organized, he added.

The responsibility for the transferred individuals will not be transferred to the African partner country in order to prevent legal action for human rights violations, but will remain with the five participating EU member states. The EU "group of five" will also finance the project entirely on its own.

There are also plans for international organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to monitor operations to ensure that international human rights standards and principles of international law are upheld.

blocks.caption: The British Supreme Court eventually stopped the push by the Conservative government to permanently deport prospective migrants to RwandaImage: Toby Melville/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Various attempts have been made in recent years to outsource asylum proceedings or deportations to countries outside the EU. None of these models worked as planned. All failed due to legal impediments, changes in government, or high costs. Below are some of the best-known precedents.
The British "Rwanda Model" (2022–2024)

The United Kingdom, under the Conservative government of Boris Johnson — and later under Rishi Sunak — sought to permanently deport migrants who had entered the country irregularly via the English Channel to Rwanda so they could undergo their asylum proceedings there.

However, the British Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal, finding that there were substantial grounds for believing that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned to countries where they could face persecution or other inhumane treatment.

Prior to that, the British government had spent £715 million (€835 million/$966 million) in taxpayer funds on the Rwanda partnership and related implementation costs. In return, a total of four people had voluntarily relocated to Rwanda

blocks.caption: Migrants in Italian return hubs in Albania had to be returned to ItalyImage: Alketa Misja/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Italy's Albania model (in place since 2024)

Under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italy signed an agreement with Albania to transport migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean directly to Italian-run centers established in Albania where expedited asylum proceedings could be conducted.

However, immediately after the camps opened, Italian courts halted the relocation. Judges argued that countries of origin such as Bangladesh or Egypt should not be classified as "safe" outright if certain groups face persecution there. These first migrants had to be returned to Italy immediately.

Italy is now using one of the camps solely as a deportation center for men whose asylum applications in Italy have been definitively rejected. Since the facility was converted in March 2025, only about 500 people have been sent there. By 2028, this comes at an estimated total cost of more than €670 million ($775 million).
Denmark's stand-alone initiatives (2021–2023)

In 2021, Denmark passed a law intended to allow asylum seekers to be flown to third countries outside the EU. Copenhagen engaged in intensive negotiations with Rwanda regarding a dedicated reception center. However, the European Commission and human rights organizations sharply criticized the initiative. In early 2023, the Danish government put the negotiations with Rwanda on hold. It became clear that the Danish plan was virtually impossible to implement legally and logistically. The government subsequently moved toward pursuing third-country return arrangements in cooperation with other European countries.
Changing legal framework

According to previous EU law, deportations to third countries often failed as courts required that a migrant have a personal connection to that third country, whether through language skills, relatives living there or a previous stay. The revised European asylum law, however, now allows individuals required to leave the EU to be transferred to a safe third country without a prior personal connection in certain circumstances — provided there is a corresponding agreement or arrangement with the third country.

A further basis for this new joint effort is the EU Return Regulation, agreed upon politically on June 17, 2026 by the Council and European Parliament. However, the regulation has not yet been formally adopted by the Council. Unlike before, the new legislation is an EU regulation and no longer merely a directive. As a result, it will apply directly once it enters into force in the EU member states bound by it. The regulation thus establishes a common EU framework for such return centers.

Furthermore, according to the new plans, the entire asylum procedure will no longer be outsourced to non-EU countries. The United Kingdom and Italy rejected this proposal. Instead, these "return hubs" will serve solely as transit stations for individuals whose asylum applications have already been legally rejected while they are financed and monitored by EU member states.

blocks.caption: Will Italy return to its migration hubs in Albania once the new EU migration pact is in place?Image: Filippo Attil/Chigi Press Office/Zumapress/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inadequate oversight and high costs?

Supporters hope that these measures will undermine the basis for human rights lawsuits regarding permanent asylum protection. Critics such as Doctors Without Borders and Amnesty International still see significant risks: They doubt that independent oversight, effective legal representation and medical care can be fully guaranteed in the hubs. They also fear that third countries could still deport people to their unsafe home countries without proper assessment.

Furthermore, experience to date shows that the construction and security of such centers, as well as the transport of those affected, often costs hundreds of millions of euro, and only a small number of people actually end up being returned.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family
articles.summary:
Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud

The International Committee of the Red Cross…

blocks.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.

More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.

The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.

Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.
Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.

“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”

blocks.caption: A Palestinian family were attacked as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in Jalud. Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPA

blocks.text: The ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. .

“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”

A bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans for even broader controls on trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.
On Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was narrowly defeated after winning backing from all but one Democrat.

“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.

A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.

More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.

blocks.caption: Mahmod Tubasi, 60, and his wife, Aedah, 51, and their family had been forced out of their homes this summer by settler militants.  Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: The Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.

Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.

“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.

Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.

The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.

blocks.caption: The Tubasi family’s homes were ‘damaged beyond description’, said Wael Tubasi. ‘Everything was broken.’ Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Earlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmert called for the international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.

Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.
A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.
An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.

“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”

On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”
