articles.title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for rejoining the EU
articles.summary:
Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit

Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks…

blocks.text: Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.

Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.

Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has said he wanted to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

Burnham used his first conference speech as the Labour leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.

The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham announced a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe in his speech at the Labour party conference. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.
Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay.

“We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”
Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.
Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”

The Guardian has learned, however, that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.
Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.

Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more, but only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.

On the same day the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.

Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will also release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.

Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pro-EU campaigners argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.

In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions, and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.
No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech, and that it was not included in any draft of it.
Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.

But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.
He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”

An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.

No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London received signals that there could be an accommodation.
Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding a summit on 20 November.
One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.
A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.

articles.title: Arizona university hockey coach put on paid leave after report on Canadian NHL prospect's collapse
articles.summary: Arizona State University hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after an anonymous letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

Arizona State University hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after an anonymous letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's review into the Hamilton-born player's collapse during an outdoor workout last month.
Hamilton-born NHL prospect still in hospital after suffering issues during Aug. 20 outdoor workout

Arizona State University (ASU) hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after a letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's review into the Canadian player's collapse during a team workout last month.

ASU athletics director Graham Rossini said in a news release Wednesday that "our focus continues to be on Matthew and his family and on our student athletes to make sure they have the support they need during this time and as the season begins.”

“We have continued to collect as much information as possible. After thorough and careful deliberation, I believe this is the best move to provide stability for the hockey program,” Rossini said about the coach being place on leave.

items: Matthew Mayich's Arizona teammates dispute school report on workout before Hamilton NHL prospect's collapse

blocks.text: In the review released last week, ASU official James Rund wrote that Hamilton-born Mayich, 21, collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined school hockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.
Mayich remains in hospital in critical condition.

items: Hockey coaches didn't submit training plan before Matthew Mayich collapsed in workout: Arizona university

blocks.text: ASU assistant hockey coach Mike Corbett will lead the team as the season opens this weekend and an interim head coach will be named soon, the release Wednesday said.
Hockey conference supports ASU's decision

ASU's move regarding Powers comes after seven members of the hockey team, in the anonymous letter sent to the university's president through their lawyer, called for the team's coaching staff to be placed on leave pending an independent investigation.

The players' letter alleges Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout on a hot day and said that, to "our knowledge, no one involved has been placed on leave, suspended or disciplined. The head coach who selected the instructor and scheduled the session continues to lead our program."
ASU is one of the 10 teams in the National Collegiate Hockey Conference (NCHC), a men's Division 1 conference in the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA).
The NCHC said in a statement that it supports ASU's decision to place Powers on leave while the circumstances surrounding Mayich's "trauma" are examined.
It said concerns raised by the student athletes "deserve to be heard and thoroughly reviewed. We will not prejudge the findings of that review."
The NCHC will stay in contact with ASU about the review and the steps being taken to protect and support student athletes, the statement said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brittany Spencer is a multi-platform reporter and producer based in Hamilton. She's previously worked with CBC in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick covering politics, health care and the justice system. She's a graduate of Toronto Metropolitan University's journalism program and joined CBC in 2017. You can reach her at brittany.spencer@cbc.ca.

articles.title: What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
articles.summary: The captain and first officer were injured, and one pilot has been arrested, officials say.

blocks.text: At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But, speaking on Wednesday following the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in northeastern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.

Passenger Yaniv Hayun, who was later greeted and described as a hero by Netanyahu, said in a video released by the prime minister's office that he and others were trying to open the cockpit door, but the stabbed pilot was very close to it.
Before the pilot collapsed, the injured man managed to open the door, Hayun said.
He said that inside, the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".
Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside of the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.

He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane, explaining to Netanyahu that he watches Canadian documentary series Air Crash Investigation. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there."
Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
"There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event," he added.
Yasmin Abukasis told Reuters that her daughter who was on the flight said a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, with blood everywhere.
"The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream, they think they are going," Abukasis told AP news agency.

Speaking from Ben Gurion Airport, she said her daughter phoned her to say she heard screaming as a pilot called for help, adding that two other pilots took control of the plane as other passengers ran towards a man who had a knife.

Almog Itali, who was also on board the flight, told media one of the pilots who landed the aircraft was British. The other pilot was European, Itali said, although he did not provide a specific nationality.
One female passenger described the "very stressful" moment people realised the plane was descending. "We understood the pilots lost control," she told Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom.
"There are people here with shirts covered in blood," she said, adding: "Now we are fine and want to return home."
Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.
Speaking later on Wednesday, Netanyahu called the situation a "a very serious security incident".
He added Israeli security forces are "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers".
"I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."

Flydubai meanwhile said "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".
The airline said two replacement aircraft were sent to Tabuk to relieve the passengers and crew, and the incident had no impact on other scheduled operations.
The repatriation flight carrying passengers left Tabuk at 17:40 local time (14:40 GMT) and arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT).

The spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."

articles.title: Stella McCartney spotlights sea life at Paris fashion week as animal rights returns to headlines
articles.summary:
Designer is developing wool alternatives and for Paris wants focus to be on ‘sea life, not sea food’ with ocean-inspired clothes

Stella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at…

blocks.text: Stella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season. Outcry over the physical restraining of a Peta protester at a catwalk show by Steven Kolb, the president of New York fashion week’s governing body, has put cruelty in wool production – previously considered a niche issue compared with the hot button topic of fur – on the news agenda.

“There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. McCartney has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Lopez and Juliette Binoche on the front row for the catwalk. Photograph: Domine Jerome/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel. At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that. But I’m alone in that, and I shouldn’t be.”

McCartney’s remarks on sustainability were interrupted by paparazzi clamouring for a portrait of the designer with the front row guest Jennifer Lopez, wearing a skirt suit with a faux-fur trim and matching stole with a dramatic black net face veil. Tension between fashion week razzmatazz and values-led gravitas is in the Stella McCartney DNA.

blocks.caption: A model on the catwalk at Stella McCartney’s Paris fashion week show. Photograph: David Fisher/Shutterstock

blocks.text: This season, McCartney’s spotlight is on sea life. “Sea life, not sea food. That’s the point I wanted to make,” she said, after posing with Lopez and dispatching Juliette Binoche with a promise to join her for a glass of champagne shortly. “I’ve never eaten fish, really, but my mum and dad used to point out that one minute people are watching a sea life documentary with David Attenborough and exclaiming about this magical world and the next, they are looking at a seafood menu. It is grotesque.”

The invitation to the show, held in the vast gardens of the British embassy in Paris, was delivered via a video message from 91-year-old Sylvia Earle, the legendary oceanographer who has spent more than 7,000 hours underwater. Fancy long-sleeved swimsuits walked the catwalk as evening looks; dolphins frolicked on T-shirts. The cursive hems of party dresses looked like Hokusai waves. “We are at war with the oceans, at war with the creatures that live in there,” McCartney said. “For every fish you eat, countless are thrown back dead.”

articles.title: France's Macron, Spain's Sanchez welcome idea of UK rejoining EU after Burnham remarks
articles.summary: During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out…

image.caption: French and Spanish leaders are warm to the idea of the UK rejoining the EU, but it's a politically fraught issue in the UK Image: Cheng Min/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday welcomed the idea of the United Kingdom rejoining the European Union.
During a visit to Madrid while meeting with Sanchez, Macron reacted to the idea of a UK rejoin with two words in English: "Welcome back."
"If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news both for his country and for Europeans," Macron continued in French.
At the same time, Macron said the UK cannot take an a la carte approach to its relationship with the EU, while remaining outside the bloc.
"You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union and decide to take what suits us and not the rest," he said.
Sanchez said the UK's decision to leave the EU as a result of a referendum in 2016 is "a huge loss, both for the British population and for the whole European project."
The Spanish prime minister said if the UK indeed does try to rejoin the EU, "then of course Spain would applaud it and open its arms again to a brotherly people."
10 years after Brexit vote: What do young Britons want now?

In a separate statement from the EU, European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said: "The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward."
"We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward," Ujvari said.
Burnham: UK should consider options in regards to EU ties
In an interview with the BBC earlier on Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain should look at various options when it comes to the relationship with the EU.
"We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," Burnham said, while saying one option would be to "go all the way."
Other possibilities might include rejoining the EU's single market or a customs union between the two sides, he said.

blocks.caption: Burnham touched on the UK's ties with the EU during an emotional address to fellow Labour Party members in Liverpool on TuesdayImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: During a speech at the annual Labour Party conference on Tuesday, Burnham said that "Brexit has done more harm than good." He added he would set out "different options" for the UK-EU relationship closer to a summit between the two sides in November.
Such a decision to move closer or rejoin the EU could open up a tense political debate in the UK.

Although recent public surveys suggest that the majority of Britons back rejoining, the idea of adopting the Euro currency or contributing to the EU budget would likely spark fierce backlash. Moreover, the UK is unlikely to receive the same exemptions it had when it was previously a member of the EU.

For now, Burnham is committed to the 2024 Labour Party manifesto, which ruled out rejoining the EU and other elements such as returning to the EU single market. However, Burnham could push Labour for a closer approach to the EU in the next general election, which is slated for no later than August 2029.

articles.title: Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?
articles.summary: It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants…

image.caption: A mural depicting shipping restrictions in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in Sanaa, YemenImage: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last week, some students in Saudi Arabia were told they should stay at home and attend classes online, due to continued threats from attacks by the Houthi group in neighboring Yemen. But the very next day, they were given the all-clear and allowed to return to school in person.

The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen seems to have become part of everyday life in Saudi Arabia. After a period of comparative calm, the Houthis have been ramping up attacks on the country, starting July, and have fired many missiles and drones over the border.

Over recent weeks, the Houthi militia have also pushed further into Yemen, taking more control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea. This means they can oversee maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

blocks.caption: A plume of smoke rises from a fuel depot at the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, after Houthi attacksImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: The renewed Houthi attacks endanger Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's ambitious project to move the kingdom away from its dependence on oil revenues, which was conceived by Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. To make Vision 2030 a reality, Saudi Arabia needs stability — but right now, the outlook is moving in the opposite direction.

"The escalation in Yemen is drawing the Saudis deeper into the regional war, a war that Saudi Arabia actually wanted to prevent," said Marcus Schneider, who heads the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Peace and Security Project in the Middle East.
Impact on world's energy

Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to Houthi attacks, which have already disrupted the so-called East-West pipeline, which runs for over 1,200 kilometers. It was being used to transport oil after other routes, such as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, became precarious due to fighting between the United States, Israel and Iran.

Houthi attacks disabled the pipeline although reports from a week ago suggest it is being used again. And thanks to the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which means "gate of tears" in English — is also coming under pressure.

Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in the Middle East program of the US think tank, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, calls it a "one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures." In fact, it may send the Saudis back to the Strait of Hormuz to try to ship their oil, even though that route is still heavily restricted.

blocks.caption: A Yemeni soldier guards an LPG tanker at the Bab al-Mandeb StraitImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who will help?

It is unlikely that Saudi ally, the US, is going to send help. Washington has said it will support the Saudis with intelligence and reconnaissance, but President Donald Trump appears reluctant to get involved in a direct military campaign against the Houthis.
According to a US-based think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, this may partially be because the it is feeling the strain of its ongoing campaign against Iran.
"The US military is reportedly facing serious challenges, including shortages of some sophisticated interceptors," the CSIS wrote in a commentary last week.
The US Council on Foreign Relations, or CFR, has also written about dwindling stocks of Patriot and interceptor missiles, as well as cruise missiles.
So the risk of opening another front in its war with Iran, in Yemen, is not a welcome prospect for the US.

As it is, US airstrikes are unlikely to resolve the Houthi problem anyway. The CFR writes that to defuse the Houthi threat, a large, coordinated ground operation is needed, especially if forces want to push the Yemeni militia back out of the areas they recently took around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia is not too enthusiastic about this either. Despite help from the US and neighboring United Arab Emirates, a Saudi coalition that fought against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022 failed to achieve any kind of decisive victory. It also demonstrated the limits of Saudi military power.

There's clear military asymmetry. Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. But the Houthis don't need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to use missiles and drones to threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping.

"The Houthis are well-established in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows," Schneider told DW. "Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, needs stability above all for its 2030 economic vision. And this is currently further away than ever."
Help from the Europeans?

Since early 2024, through what is known as Operation Aspides, Europe has been protecting international shipping in the Red Sea. Italy has recently said it intends to secure passage for its own merchant ships with its navy. And a few days ago France said it would send soldiers, radar systems and air defense to the Saudis in order to protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the terminus of the East-West pipeline.

Still, these European initiatives are unlikely to bring about any sort of strategic shift in Yemen. And experts argue Europe is unwilling to accept the political and military cost of a protracted war there.

blocks.caption: The new Mecca alliance: A meeting of military chiefs from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, held in Saudi Arabia in September this yearImage: Turkish Defence Ministry/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The fact that France has now announced it will provide concrete military assistance has been received very positively in Riyadh," Schneider explained. "But still the question remains as to whether this can fundamentally alter the military balance."

The recently formed mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, known as the Mecca alliance, also has its limits. The military leaders of all three countries have consulted with one another over recent Houthis attacks but Turkey and Pakistan are also reluctant to be drawn into a conflict that would see them confronting Iran directly.
Diplomacy the way forward
All this means that diplomatic overtures will likely become more important again.
In a previous interview with DW, Abdulghani al-Iryani of the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies noted that the Houthis do actually have an interest in relations with Saudi Arabia.
"Yemen is completely economically dependent on Saudi Arabia, both as a source of humanitarian aid and as a labor market for Yemeni migrant workers," al-Iryani said.

In recent years, Saudi Arabia has tried to curb the Houthis' influence through diplomacy and by uniting divided Yemeni government forces. However the militia's current advance seems to demonstrate the limitations of this strategy.
This story was originally published in German.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?

articles.title: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster
articles.summary: Thirty-one migrants died when their boat went down in November 2021. The trial found that the guilty men were part of two smuggling networks.

blocks.text: Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.
At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years.
Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty.

The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived.

The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets".

The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks – one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan – that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point.
Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat.

Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims".

One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him."
Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving.

"I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said.

The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower.

The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves."
His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating".
Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks.
The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure.
The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network – named as Bashdar – was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide – Harem Ahmed Abawaker – was given eight years in prison.
The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant.
Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants.
A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster.

The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months.

The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum.

France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model.

articles.title: Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
articles.summary: The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?

image.caption: Expressions of Jewish identity, such as wearing a kippah, have become more rare in Berlin due to antisemitic incidents (file photo from 2023)Image: Michele Tantussi/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election on September 20. This means there's a good chance that the party's top candidate, Elif Eralp, could become Berlin's next mayor — making her the first member of the Left Party to hold that office.

Preliminary talks with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the environmentalist Green Party are scheduled to take place on October 1. If the talks are successful, it would represent a major step toward forming a coalition government.

Securing a clear commitment from the Left Party against antisemitism within its own ranks is seen as a prerequisite for successful cooperation. Yet doubts still persist about whether the party and its representatives can adequately protect Jewish life in the city.

During the election campaign, a performance at a Left Party event by the rapper Dahabflex made headlines and sparked outrage when he used slogans seen as antisemitic during his performance. And later, at an event held by the Left Party to celebrate its election victory, an appearance was made by Ibrahim Ibrahim — a supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is on the EU's list of terrorist organizations. The leaders of the Left Party have repeatedly distanced themselves from both incidents, both at the federal and state levels.
German Left Party co-chair on allegations of antisemitism
The Central Council of Jews in Germany is warning
However, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, thinks these statements are mere lip service.

"In the fight against antisemitism, which is tolerated and allowed to run rampant within the party's ranks, the Left Party no longer has any credibility," reads a press statement released two days after the election. Schuster explicitly appealed to the SPD and the Greens not to form a coalition with the election winner.

High-ranking members of the federal government have also spoken out. Wolfram Weimer, government commissioner for culture and media who has no party affiliation, accused the Left Party of "openly flaunting antisemitism" and called into question the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in funding for the capital's cultural sector for the coming decade — a deal that had already been agreed upon with the Berlin state government. Weimer claimed that many figures in the cultural sector are alarmed by the prospect of a government led by the Left Party.
'Antisemitism and expropriations threaten the economy'

Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also voiced concern. A video titled "Antisemitism and Expropriations Threaten the Economy" is available on her ministry's Instagram account, in reference also to the Left Party's plans to nationalize large private housing companies.

Reiche describes the Left as a party "that openly embraces antisemitism, that instills fear in the Jews of this city, that opposes Jewish life and that cheerfully welcomes organized crime at election parties."
The Left Party is now seeking an injunction to compel the Minister of Economic Affairs to delete the video.
"Reiche is using taxpayer money to spread propaganda against the Left Party on the Economy Ministry's official channel," said Left Party Federal Co-Chair Ines Schwerdtner.
150 prominent Jews come to the defense of the Left Party

In an open letter, a group of 150 prominent Jews from various social backgrounds has voiced support for the Left Party. Among those who signed it are the author Eva Menasse and the former director of the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Susan Neiman. They advocate for a "social and safe city" and emphasize the importance of voting for different parties.

They explain their motivation as follows: "We are writing this letter because, over the past few weeks, we have heard the same claim time and again: that the Left is dangerous for Jews, and that a coalition involving the party poses a danger to our safety. We reject this claim not because we downplay concerns about our safety, but because we actually take them seriously."

Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."

In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."
Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?

The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.
Elif Eralp wants to build bridges

Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.

The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.
"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."
With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.
"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.

blocks.caption: Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York, rejects sweeping accusations of antisemitism against the Left PartyImage: DW

blocks.text: Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.
One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.

"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."

Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison officially signals his intent to resign later this fall
articles.summary: Ontario MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison said Wednesday that he intends to resign his seat at the end of the fall sitting.

image.caption: MP for Parry Sound–Muskoka Scott Aitchison rises during Question Period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Jan. 28, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Ontario MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison said Wednesday that he intends to resign his seat at the end of the fall sitting.
Ontario MP and former mayor made bid for Conservative leadership in 2022
"After 30 years of public life, it is time for a new chapter where I will explore new opportunities," Aitchison wrote in a social media post.

Aitchison — a former mayor of Huntsville, Ont., who has been MP for the Parry Sound–Muskoka riding since 2019 — didn't indicate what his next steps will be. But he reflected on his time in public office and thanked his constituents and staff.

"I worked to build consensus, cut through the bureaucracy, and make life better for the people who placed their trust in me," he wrote. "I carried myself with the same values of the town that raised me: respect, decency, and looking out for your neighbour."
CBC News reported Tuesday that Aitchison had intended to step down this fall. CTV News first confirmed the news of his departure.
Conservative MP Scott Aitchison to step down: sources
Aitchson launched a leadership bid in the 2022 Conservative campaign that saw Pierre Poilievre chosen as the party's chief, where he finished fifth.
Housing was a key feature of Aitchison's leadership campaign and Poilievre named the MP as his housing critic — something he reflected on in his statement.

"All levels of government have recognized the burden over-regulation and excessive taxes and fees place on housing affordability. Our Conservative team can be proud of the work we have done on this file and I know the team will continue this work after my departure," he wrote.

"To my caucus colleagues and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, it has been a privilege to serve alongside you. I have been fortunate to meet Canadians from coast to coast who are counting on us to champion efforts to make life more affordable for all Canadians."
Poilievre praised Aitchison as "a friend, a dedicated public servant and a man who cares deeply about the people he represents."
"Scott Aitchison has spent his life serving the community and country he loves," the Conservative leader wrote in a social media post.

"Scott's greatest strength has always been his connection to his home. Whether fighting for local workers and businesses, helping people navigate the federal government, or championing a community fund to support housing, food security and mental health in Parry Sound–Muskoka, he never forgot who sent him to Ottawa."
Aitchison's resignation will create another vacancy in the House, where six seats are currently empty.

Aitchison's fellow Conservatives Larry Brock and Cathay Wagantall both stepped down in the past month. Their vacancies are coupled with former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault, who officially resigned last month, and former Liberal MP Shaun Chen, who resigned in mid-August.
Former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice and the Bloc Québécois's Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay both stepped away from federal politics to run in Quebec's upcoming provincial election.

While the clock is ticking for those six byelections to be called, Aitchison's seat won't be open until he makes his resignation official at the end of this sitting. Parliament is scheduled to sit until Dec. 11.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Fined telcos ask NTC for due process
articles.summary: The country’s biggest telcos are asking the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to observe due process after they were slapped with a daily fine of P100,000 over internet quality.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

In a statement, the Philippine Chamber of Telecommunication Operators (PCTO), made up of companies including PLDT Inc. and Globe Telecom Inc., demanded the NTC extend due process to telcos before handing out penalties.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The country’s biggest telcos are asking the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to observe due process after they were slapped with a daily fine of P100,000 over internet quality.
The PCTO said the NTC has started charging fines over internet quality upon the issuance of show-cause orders.
The telcos were unable to air their side and contest the findings. Further, they questioned the process by which the NTC had arrived at the conclusion that their internet services are poor.

The PCTO said it recognizes the NTC’s memorandum circular requiring periodic audits on telco performance. However, the NTC has yet to outline the methodologies for the audit, from actual metrics to testing conditions.
“Operators should not be penalized under standards that have not been clearly defined and have not been consistently applied,” the PCTO said.
The telcos flagged the government for regulatory uncertainty and its penalty regime, as resources have to be diverted to paying fines instead of network investments.
They also attacked the NTC for failing to address longstanding issues on the local level, ranging from varying local government permitting to costly charges and lengthy approvals.
PLDT, Globe and Dito Telecommunity Corp. were imposed a P100,000 a day penalty until such time they have upgraded network assets to improve internet coverage in certain areas.
Globe was told to step up efforts in Makati and Quezon City; PLDT unit Smart Communications Inc. in Manila, Parañaque and Pasig and Dito, in Las Piñas, Pasay and San Juan.

articles.title: Bonoan remains accused in graft case
articles.summary: Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan will remain as Sen. Jinggoy Estrada’s co-accused in a graft case linked to the flood control controversy.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Former Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan attends the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee hearing on the flood control controversy on Monday, January 19, 2026.
Senate PRIB / Released
MANILA, Philippines — Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan will remain as Sen. Jinggoy Estrada’s co-accused in a graft case linked to the flood control controversy.
The Sandiganbayan Second Division has affirmed its ruling denying prosecutors’ bid to drop Bonoan as a defendant.
Bonoan is accused of conspiring with Estrada to ensure that flood control projects in Bulacan were included in the 2025 national budget.
Estrada allegedly received P213.7 million in kickbacks.
In a separate plunder case involving Estrada, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division had dropped Bonoan as co-accused and released him from detention.
Bonoan is out on bail.
The ombudsman earlier asked the courts to drop the charges against Bonoan so he could be considered a state witness.

During pre-trial, Estrada’s lawyers said they will mark as evidence former Bulacan district engineer Brice Hernandez’s affidavit, which stated that Estrada lacked participation in the alleged kickback scheme.
Brice pleads not guilty
Hernandez and six others have pleaded not guilty to graft charges involving an alleged P77-million ghost flood control project in Balagtas, Bulacan.

Before the anti-graft court’s Fifth Division, Hernandez and former public works officials Jaypee Mendoza, Arjay Domaig, Niño Morales, Juanito Mendoza, Floralyn Simbulan and Christina Pineda entered their not-guilty pleas.
Three others were not arraigned since they are still at large, namely former lawmaker and fugitive Zaldy Co and his staff members John Paul Estrada and Mark Tecsay.
The P77-million flood control project was declared 100 percent complete by May 2025 even though it only started in February 2025.
The structure did not exist, according to the Office of the Ombudsman.
Rep. Rivera suspended
Tarlac Rep. Noel Rivera has been suspended for 90 days over alleged conflict of interest in government infrastructure projects.

Facing two graft cases, Rivera is accused of maintaining financial interests in nine infrastructure projects awarded to Tarlac 3-G Construction and Development Corp. during his term as lawmaker from 2022 to 2025.
Rivera is one of the alleged “cong-tractors” involved in the flood control scam.
Rivera allegedly owned a controlling stake in the firm, which won a P94.86-million contract in 2023 for a road project in San Narcisco, Zambales.

articles.title: Palace tells Velasco to face probe; houses raided
articles.summary: Malacañang has advised former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco to come forward and shed light on the allegations against him after the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that he left the…

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

Image shows dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (center) with former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and Vice President Sara Duterte. This is one of the photographs included with the affidavit Gracioso submitted to the NBI.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has advised former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco to come forward and shed light on the allegations against him after the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that he left the country on Aug. 30 and did not come home on his expected date of return.?

Velasco may clear the air after dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., the lawmaker’s former security officer, claimed in an affidavit that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members of her family, including her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is now probing the claims of Gracioso, who alleged that the cash deliveries, in suitcases, were made upon Velasco’s orders.

Velasco’s camp has denied the allegations, saying Gracioso’s “one-size-fits-all narration” appears to be “designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events.”?
The BI said Velasco flew to Japan on Aug. 30 and did not return to Manila on Sept. 14, his date of arrival.

“Whether he is afraid or is just taking a vacation, we cannot tell. But if his name is mentioned in the millions contained in suitcases allegedly delivered to the Vice President, (former) president Duterte and Congressman Pulong Duterte, it would be better if he sheds light on it so he can clear his name and that of his wife,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a media briefing yesterday.
The NBI intends to invite people named in Gracioso’s affidavit, including Velasco’s wife, Rowena, who reportedly left the country on Sept. 24.
Gracioso yesterday underwent a lie detector test at the NBI. Results have not been published yet.
In a 1978 decision, the Supreme Court said it “does not put much faith and credit on” a lie detector test.
NBI raids houses
NBI agents with a search warrant raided houses allegedly owned by Velasco in Valle Verde, Pasig on Aug. 24, according to NBI Director Melvin Matibag.
Matibag told reporters on Tuesday that operatives initially didn’t know that the properties belonged to Velasco because they were registered under the names of his employees and a certain company.
Operatives seized firearms, bullets, magazines and IDs belonging to police and security personnel.
Former lawmaker Mikee Romero claimed in a Facebook post on Sept. 25 that Velasco’s home was being raided “now” by the NBI.
However, it was unclear whether it was a separate raid that Romero referred to or the same one that Matibag had confirmed. – EJ Macababbad

articles.title: Digital platform launched for anti-dynasty law initiative
articles.summary: The People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasty, through its Dapat Isa Lang initiative, launched a digital signature platform yesterday in its push to end political dynasties.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasty (PICAD), through its Dapat Isa Lang initiative, launched a digital signature platform yesterday in its push to end political dynasties.
PICAD convenor Eirene Aguila said the initiative aims to collect 7.5 million signatures, with 10 percent coming from registered voters nationwide and the other three percent from each district.
She said the digital platform is “a vehicle to exercise constitutional power” and is not a form of rebellion but “democracy in the most peaceful form.”
“In a people’s initiative, we’re not just mere voters. We help in shaping the law,” she said.
Dapat Isa Lang initially used to collect signatures manually, but it was halted when the coalition decided to move it to a digital platform to be more inclusive.
“The goal is inclusivity. We want everyone’s participation in this campaign,” Karlo Abadines, head of Dapat Isa Lang stated.
When asked about the accessibility, he said they already talked to their partners to organize digital kiosks.
“You can invite community members to go to our partner schools, churches. Our personnel will help them and will provide devices for them to sign the petition,” Abadines said.
PICAD chairman Antonio Carpio demonstrated the step-by-step process on how to sign the petition online through d1l.org.
According to him, the entire process may only last three minutes.

Speaking at the launch of the digital signature platform, former Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman and member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission Christian Monsod said gathering 7.3 million signatures in four months is “a huge, huge task.”
“We will help you in this task because we know it’s a difficult one,” he declared.
During his speech, Monsod admitted he initially proposed that the ban on political dynasties should no longer be included in the current Charter but he later withdrew it.

“During the deliberations by the Constitutional Commission on this issue, I myself said ‘wait, if you have this prohibition on dynasties, maybe there are those who are good and honest who happen to belong to a political family and we’re saying he cannot run because of this anti-dynasty provision,’” he said.
While on recess, he said he realized the need to retain the anti-political dynasty provision after discussions with fellow members of the commission.
For instance, such a ban was a “cost and benefit issue” and that it would “open the door to the millions of poor Filipinos who deserve to be in public office,” he said.

Also, the ban on political dynasties would “close the door on the circumvention of the term limits,” especially with succession of family members in elective positions, and at the same time promote “equitable distribution of power for the common good.”
Eventually, Monsod said he “withdrew” his proposal to exclude the political dynasty ban.
Suspension lifted
The Comelec has lifted its suspension on the rules governing people’s initiative for legislative amendments, Chairman George Garcia said on Tuesday.

Speaking at the Kapihan sa Manila Bay forum, he said the Comelec had previously suspended its rules covering both constitutional and legislative amendments, but later lifted the suspension on legislative matters following discussions with Congress.
Garcia said the move means there is no longer a procedural barrier for groups seeking to use a people’s initiative to push for legislation, including a proposed ban on political dynasties.
However, Garcia noted that the Comelec still has to address the use of electronic signatures, which are not currently covered by its existing rules on people’s initiative.
Meanwhile, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) reminded barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials that the extension of their term is not an exemption from liabilities.
The DILG said longer term means greater responsibility and accountability, and officials should not take advantage of their extended tenure.

The department said it would continue guiding and provide technical assistance to barangay and SK officials to ensure they remain responsive to their constituents’ needs. – Ghio Ong, Christine Boton, Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities
articles.summary:
Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews,…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.

As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”

The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.

Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.

Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.

Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.

Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.

blocks.caption: Students’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.

“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”

Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.

“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”

Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.

Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.

She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”

The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.

“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”

Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.

Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”

Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

articles.title: African leaders herald $16B Dangote oil refinery in Kenya
articles.summary: An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.

image.caption: Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni and Kenya’s President William Ruto made a symbolic ceremony dig to celebrate the projectImage: Luis Tato/AFP

blocks.text: African leaders on Wednesday broke ground on a new $16 billion (€14 billion) oil refinery off Kenya's coast.
The project is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. The refinery will be constructed at the coastal town of Lamu.

Kenya's President William Ruto, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed were among the leaders who attended an event to celebrate the project, the largest of its kind in East and Central Africa.
The refinery "will strengthen regional energy security, reduce reliance on imports and bolster our foreign exchange," Ruto said on social media.
"But this is more than a refinery. It is an integrated industrial complex featuring a 1,000MW power plant, plastic factory and the manufacturing of fertilizers and chemicals."
Africa's richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, will oversee the project.
Dangote: Project will reduce refined fuel imports, foster self-sufficiency
Dangote said the refinery will make East Africa more "self-sufficient" by reducing imports of refined fuel.
"For too long, our continent has actually been rich in resources but poor in value creation and addition. We have exported crude oil and imported refined products," Dangote said in his speech.

"Such practice only leads to us exporting our jobs and opportunities that should remain on the continent and lead us into importing poverty into our nations. Africa cannot build lasting prospertiy by exporting what it has and importing what it needs," he continued.

blocks.caption: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote (right) inspected earthmoving machinery with Kenyan President William Ruto (left)Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Lamu project faces environmental concerns, legal challenge
The project, however, has faced resistance from environmental campaigners who fear it could harm Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site which also hosts a fragile and unique marine ecosystem.
The Lamu marine environment is also home to animals such as dugongs, whales and various sea turtle species.

blocks.caption: The Lamu region is home to an incredible variety of aquatic life [FILE: October 4, 2011] Image: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS

blocks.text: Lamu residents have brought a land rights legal case against the refinery, saying the site where it will be built is their ancestral heritage.
Kenya's High Court on Monday ruled that legal proceedings will continue, but the groundbreaking ceremony can take place.

articles.title: After last-minute stay, U.S. Supreme Court says Tennessee can execute Christa Pike
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court is allowing the execution of Christa Gail Pike to go forward, overturning a last-minute stay on Wednesday that was issued by an appeals court hours earlier.

image.caption: Christa Pike is shown on Jan. 12, 2023, in this photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

blocks.text: World·Updated
The U.S. Supreme Court is allowing the execution of Christa Gail Pike to go forward, overturning a last-minute stay on Wednesday that was issued by an appeals court hours earlier.
Pike, now 50, was convicted for a murder she committed at age 18

Pike was scheduled to die by lethal injection in the morning, and witnesses had already gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike's allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.
Pike, now 50, and her boyfriend were convicted of stabbing and beating 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility, in Knoxville in 1995.

The Sixth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals halted Pike's execution on a 2-1 vote about an hour before the scheduled execution time, as witnesses and others gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.

The case garnered widespread attention at the time in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and '90s.
Attorney general challenges appeal

Tennessee's attorney general immediately appealed the stay to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media remained at the prison while the high court considered whether to allow the execution to proceed.

The state's execution order expires at midnight, said Kelley Henry, a Nashville-based lawyer experienced with Tennessee death penalty law. If time runs out and the stay is lifted, the Tennessee Supreme Court would need to set a new execution date.

In its appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, the attorney general's office wrote that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer's family and rewarded "abusive delay tactics" by Pike's lawyers.

Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters have argued the state should consider her age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler.

"It is inconceivable that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant's moral culpability," her lawyers wrote in a filing to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Renewed debate

As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds sentenced to death in Tennessee have had their sentences vacated.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on."

items: Florida carries out record 16th execution of the year, for child murderer sentenced to death in 1980

blocks.text: "I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.
"Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez said in a telephone interview.
Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution. She didn't respond to a message on Wednesday after the execution was halted.
Martinez said her daughter's age also should matter in deciding Pike's fate.

items: U.S. executes 1st woman on federal death row in nearly 7 decades

blocks.text: "Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said, noting that her daughter would have turned 51 earlier in September.
The 1995 killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995.

Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Tadaryl Shipp, Pike's boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Executions of women rare in U.S.

Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it's difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.
It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about one per cent of all executions, according to the centre.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S.
In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.
Pike would be the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.
