articles.title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations
articles.summary: The government authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and dozens of other wild animals for independence day feasts.

blocks.text: Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.
The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain.
A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23celephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes".
The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection.
He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government.
"Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said.

Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread.
Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead.

He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations.

Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events.
The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations.
The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country.
It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment.
But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat.

In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school.

He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution.

"For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass.
Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple.
Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt.
The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population.
Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people.
The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities.
The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi.
Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024.
The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development.
Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found.
But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable.

Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants.
They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements.

articles.title: Top Trump figures push to direct human rights funding to rightwing causes
articles.summary:
Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights

With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is…
articles.byline: Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington

blocks.text: With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a massive $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court, and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilisational norms”.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while likely angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which makes up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire human rights and democracy fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe, and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human-rights defenders and civil-society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The largest award of $40m was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus, and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but told the Guardian the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals.”

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the State Department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, on issues from online safety law to migration that are live in British politics.

articles.title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.summary: At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, local authorities reported.

blocks.text: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said.
At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, including a child in the Kyiv region, local authorities reported.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. This has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials.
In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.

In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. It is not clear if the three he mentioned included the child.
Two people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region, governor Oleh Hryhorov said, while another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
articles.summary: The withdrawal of coalition forces, under a deal agreed two years ago, was a key demand of the Iraqi government.

blocks.text: The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.
The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.
It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.

British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".
Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.

"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.
"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".

He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."
The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.
A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".
The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.
Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.
But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.
Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.
Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.
A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.
They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.
At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.

RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.

It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.

It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.
The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.
US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.
US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.
This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.
Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.

They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.
The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.
US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

articles.title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, says Tokyo court
articles.summary:
Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark verdict to protect publicity rights

A court in Japan has ruled that the human…

blocks.text: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.

Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.

But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.

The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.

Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.

The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.

The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.

At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
after newsletter promotion
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.

TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.
With reporting by Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Couple describes relief at rescue after whale destroys their yacht
articles.summary: Jeremy and Gemma Cooper were 500 miles off the coast of New Zealand when their yacht, the Tai Tam, collided with a sperm whale.

blocks.text: A sailor couple have spoken of their relief to be rescued after a sperm whale collided with their yacht.

Jeremy and Gemma Cooper told the BBC that they were 500 nautical miles off the coast of New Zealand when the boat, the Tai Tam, lurched port side and they knew they'd "been hit by something" - only to see a pod of six sperm whales swimming behind the boat.
As their boat took on water and eventually sank, the Coopers and two other sailors aboard the vessel evacuated to a life raft. Seventeen hours later they were rescued by a container ship.
The couple told the BBC that, despite their ordeal, they would be out on the water again soon.
Video produced by Lana Lam, edited by Alex Foster.

articles.title: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
articles.summary: Indonesian lawmakers on Wednesday ordered the demolition of a controversial luxury compound inside a penitentiary near the capital.

blocks.text: A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments within the penitentiary.
Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September.

The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.

The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

articles.title: Commercial plane travelling from Dubai to Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia after distress call
articles.summary: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible…

image.caption: A FlyDubai jet, not involved in the diversion to Saudi Arabia, is shown at Dubai International Airport in October 2024. Another of the carrier's planes transmitted an emergency alert Wednesday shortly after takeoff, according to publicly available flight tracking information. (Jon Gambrell/The Assoc

blocks.text: World·New

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes. A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots.
Alert sparks fear of hijacking, but incident involved fight in cockpit among pilots, reports say

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.

Israeli media, citing security officials, said the incident stemmed from a feud between the plane's two pilots, and everyone on board was safe. The plane landed in Tabuk, a civilian and military base in the kingdom.
The FlyDubai plane transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff, according to publicly available flight-tracking information.
A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots. It wasn't immediately clear what had caused the fight, the official said.
Israel scrambles warplanes

A second official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking of a plane carrying dozens of its citizens. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was still under investigation.

Flights resume after ground stops at major U.S. airports, including New York's JFK and ‌LaGuardia

blocks.text: Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare, yet not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-Paris flight, though it did not have to be diverted and landed as planned.
Plane dipped steeply, passengers say

Passengers on the plane told Israel's Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouts from passengers toward the front of the plane who heard the altercation between the pilots, and the plane dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia.
They also said that all the passengers were staying on the plane and that there was a heavy presence of Saudi security forces surrounding them.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines. The U.A.E. has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020.
According to Flight Radar, the incident occurred about 2½ hours after takeoff.
FlyDubai later confirmed that Flight FZ 1073, en route to Ben Gurion, experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday.
"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," the carrier said. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."

Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including often invasive check-in procedures for Israel-bound flights.

articles.title: Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
articles.summary: The launch of FirstDate comes as the ageing nation wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.

blocks.text: Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.

FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads.
Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values.
FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot.
On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme.
The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences.

The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things.

"At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC.
"But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?"
But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government.
Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise.
"Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user.
It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment.
The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025.
The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025.

In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17.
FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens.
In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle.

Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out.
The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates.

The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate.
The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

articles.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
articles.summary: Israeli media say authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane before it diverted to Saudi Arabia.

image.caption: Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities are investigating whether a pilot on a Flydubai flight tried to crash the Israel-bound on Wednesday, according to Israeli media reports.
The plane lost thousands of meters of altitude in about a minute before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, with Flydubai confirming that all passengers were safe.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.
"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.
Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots.
According to reports, the captain was of Russian origin and the co-pilot Ukrainian.

articles.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
articles.summary: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.

image.caption: From now on, the US president wants AI to be referred to as 'Super Intelligence'Image: Imaginechina-Tuchong/IMAGO

blocks.text: What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).

Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.

In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
How US, China could end the AI race
'AI is not superintelligence'

The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.

"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."

Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.

Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."

Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.
Rebrand won't quell AI fears

"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. “If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."

Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.
A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.

Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.
The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.

blocks.caption: Current AI models are smart but won't meet the superintelligence criteria for yearsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A branding gift to help the AI boom?

Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.

Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.ran tasks they were not meant to.

With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.

"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it’s playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."
The future of AI: Who's really controlling it?
Superintelligence remains a moving target

While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.

On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.

Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.

Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.

At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.

"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

articles.title: Ireland will boycott Eurovision again because of Israel's participation, but the song contest is still expanding
articles.summary: The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.

image.caption: Bulgaria's Darina Nikolaeva Yotova, aka Dara, won the contest this year with the song 'Bangaranga' Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP

blocks.text: "Bringing the world together through music has always been an incredibly powerful idea and has stood the test of time for 70 years," Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green told DW on the sidelines of the event's annual European Broadcasting Union (EBU) workshop held in mid-September. "And I think the more difficult the world gets around us, the more important these shows of unity, these shows of togetherness become."
While Green is intent on promoting the unity of the international music contest that celebrated its 70th anniversary in May, the 2026 event was also infamously marked by unprecedented backlash.

Political boycotts over Israel's inclusion amid the war in Gaza led to a significant low point in participation and viewership, dropping from 166 million viewers in 2025 down to 131 million viewers a year later.

blocks.caption: There were also protests against Israel's participation during the contest held in Vienna in May 2026Image: Max Slovencik/APA/AFP

blocks.text: The 2027 song contest is set to remain affected by geopolitics.

Of the five countries which boycotted the 2026 event — the Netherlands, Spain, Iceland, Slovenia and Ireland — the latter has already confirmed that it will not participate for the second time in a row.

The Netherlands' usual Eurovision broadcaster had also announced it would be snubbing the show again, stating it refused to take part in an event that "can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict." Now, Dutch public broadcasting association NPO decided to step in and resume participation in the contest.
The three other countries that pulled out in 2026 have yet to make an official announcement for 2027.
Broadcasters have until mid-October 2026 to withdraw their application without facing a financial penalty.
Some adjustments made amid the crisis

In August, the contest organizers announced new rules, according to which "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," they said in a statement.

The winning country usually earns the right to host the following edition, though the United Kingdom hosted the 2023 event on behalf of Ukraine due to Russia's war on Ukraine. Even though the rule doesn't name the country, it clearly aims to avoid having the show held in Israel, which came close to taking home the trophy in 2025 and 2026.

blocks.caption: Image: Klaus Titzer/APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Organizers also plan to introduce changes to reduce politically motivated voting.
The current system allows viewers to vote up to 10 times per payment method for their favorite act, by phone, text message or online.

There was a huge uproar in 2025 when the Israeli government encouraged Israelis to register multiple votes for its contestant. The controversy had already led to a change in the voting rules; the maximum number of public votes was halved from 20 to 10.
Now the plan is to move the vote entirely online, with a system that would require people to select three acts instead of one.
Bulgaria already at work for 2027
Since Bulgarian singer Dara won in Vienna with her song "Bangaranga," her country will be hosting the event next year.
The competition will take place in Burgas, a city on the Black Sea coast.

When the city's selection was announced, people in Burgas celebrated with spontaneous music and dance performances and flash mobs, said Milena Milotinova, general director of Bulgaria's public broadcaster BNT, host of the televised event.
"I'm glad that people in Bulgaria are actually so passionate about Eurovision," Milotinova told DW. "This will be the first time Bulgaria has organized such a large-scale event at such a high level."
The Balkan country participated for the first time in 2005. It now needs to quickly develop its infrastructure for the international event.
"The important thing is that we already have a hall, and the stage design is being developed based on that," said Milotinova.
"We are in the midst of frantic preparations," she added. "There are no days off, so we hope we'll be able to get everything done on time and put on a spectacular, world-class Eurovision show."

blocks.caption: Burgas is already in Eurovision feverImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Expanding the Eurovision brand

Beyond blows to the contest's viewership, Eurovision also had to deal with a substantial financial setback due to the withdrawal of Spain, which was traditionally one of the so-called "big five" contributors supporting the event.
Yet amid these challenges, Eurovision organizers are working to expand the brand's international reach.

The Eurovision Song Contest Asia will debut in November this year, with Thailand's capital Bangkok selected as the host city for its inaugural edition. Eleven countries are taking part, and negotiations are underway to get more Asian countries to join in 2027.
A Latin American spin-off of the format has been announced in the past but has not yet materialized.
"We're always investigating new areas of the world that we can take the show to," said Martin Green. "We're beavering away on all sorts of ideas."

blocks.caption: Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green promotes the show as a symbol of 'unity' and 'togetherness'Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canada joins the party

One achievement organizers are definitely celebrating is Canada's addition to the European lineup, which was announced in July: "We are so happy that the Canadians chose to join our family," said the Eurovision Song Contest director.

Participation is not restricted to Europe's geographic boundaries; it's open to active members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Israel's public broadcaster has competed regularly since 1973. Due to its massive fan base, Australia first joined as a special participant in 2015 and has remained a committed contestant since.

"We're learning about what this takes, but we're going to put our best foot forward and really show the world what Canada can do," Jennifer Dettman, Canada's Eurovision Song Contest head of delegation, told DW.

blocks.caption: Canada can already boast some Eurovision glory: Quebec singer Celine Dion won the contest in 1988, singing for SwitzerlandImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The participation also marks a strategic push by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to deepen cultural and diplomatic ties with Europe. His government's budget included $150 million Canadian (€93 million, $106 million) in funding for the broadcaster.
"This is the biggest global music event. So it's an opportunity to put our artists on this global stage," added Dettman. "People are really excited to do that."
Jakov Leon conducted the interviews.
Canada to join 2027 Eurovision Song Contest

"She was a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance," the family said in a statement to Page Six, external and People, external.

articles.title: 'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
articles.summary: In the emotional letter, the judge describes the survivor as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

blocks.text: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.

Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).

At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage".

"When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor.

"Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.
Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth".
"The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again.
"The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."

Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".

Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.

It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.

Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.

The child abuse survivor fighting to save others

blocks.text: The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.
Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.

The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external.
And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.
Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.
In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.
After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

articles.title: Africa's richest man to launch Kenya oil refinery despite land protests
articles.summary: The Kenya refinery is part of Dangote's ambitious bid to expand and help industralise Africa by 2030.
articles.byline: Ondiro Oganga, Nkechi Ogbonna, Waihiga Mwaura, Peter Mwangangi

blocks.text: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.
Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity.
Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.
Speaking to the BBC, Dangote dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.
The Lamu refinery is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway. East Africa does not currently have any oil refineries.

In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available.

"To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.
At the height of construction, Dangote, who is Africa's richest man, said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project.
"Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.

Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline.
But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region.
"Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.
Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example.
"Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.
The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant.

Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.

He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.
In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area.
"The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.

Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.

The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria, with construction due to begin on 1 November. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day.
Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1b earlier this month.

articles.title: Germany news: Volkswagen ends collective wage agreements
articles.summary: In an effort to cut costs, automaker Volkswagen terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany. This could reignite disputes with employee representatives. DW has more.

image.caption: VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo has predicted a 'bitter dispute at the turn of the year'Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 30, 2026
Volkswagen terminates almost all collective wage agreements
German automaker Volkswagen has terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany, potentially renewing bitter disputes with employee representatives as the company seeks to cut costs.
Following a meeting with employee representatives in Hanover on Wednesday, the company announced that various provisions in the agreements would need to be adjusted in light of cost pressures.

By terminating the agreements by December 31, 2026, Volkswagen aims to open up room for negotiation. The employment security provisions agreed upon in 2024 and set to last until the end of 2030 will not be affected.
German union leaders have expressed their opposition to Volkswagen, accusing the company of declaring "war" on its staff and threatening strikes in response.
"This is a foul blow against the workforce and once again a shameless attempt to reach into employees' pockets," said IG Metall union official Thorsten Gröger.
Meanwhile, VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo predicted a "bitter dispute at the turn of the year."

Earlier this month, the carmaker and unions reached an agreement to eliminate a total of 100,000 jobs across the entire 10-marque group by the end of the decade. This is the largest restructuring in the history of the global auto industry.
Can Volkswagen stage an automotive comeback?

articles.title: Could the Parti Québécois actually abolish the monarchy in Quebec?

image.caption: Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he wants to abolish the monarchy in Quebec. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he wants to defund the office of the lieutenant-governor and pass a law to sever the province's ties to the Crown. But is a phaseout of the monarchy constitutionally feasible in Quebec?
Experts say proposal would face constitutional challenges
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he wants to defund the office of the lieutenant-governor and pass a law to sever the province's ties to the British monarchy.
"A Parti Québécois government will abolish whatever monarchy exists in Quebec," St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters Tuesday.

St-Pierre Plamondon, whose party is leading in the polls ahead of the Oct. 5 election, promised to redirect the office's budget toward combatting homelessness. This year, the office has a budget of $1.3 million.
But is a phaseout of the monarchy feasible?
It would be far from easy, according to constitutional experts. They say the PQ's plan would face legal challenges, and attempting to bypass the Crown could paralyze the province's legislature.
In Quebec, King Charles is represented by Lt.-Gov. Manon Jeannotte, whose principal constitutional duty is granting royal assent to bills passed by the National Assembly.

Section 41(a) of the Constitution Act, 1982, stipulates that any modifications to the office of the King, the Governor General or the lieutenant-governor must be approved by the House of Commons, the Senate and all 10 provincial legislatures.
Legal experts cast doubt on feasibility
Karine Millaire, an expert in constitutional law and an associate professor at the Université de Montréal, said a unilateral move by the province would be unconstitutional.
And cutting the office's funding to the point the lieutenant-governor could no longer do their job would also be legally perilous, she told CBC News.
She pointed to the Supreme Court of Canada's landmark 2014 ruling on Senate reform, which explicitly prohibits the "indirect abolition" of core institutions.
The top court ruled that governments cannot do indirectly what the Constitution forbids doing directly, she said.
Jean-François Gaudreault-DesBiens, a law professor at the Université de Montréal, also said the legal path would be difficult.
"As long as Quebec is part of Canada, I don't see how Paul St-Pierre Plamondon could achieve his goals through a simple law passed by the National Assembly," he told Radio-Canada.
Another legal expert noted that if a PQ government attempted to bypass the lieutenant-governor, it could put the validity of any new legislation into doubt.

Any bills passed by the National Assembly that failed to receive royal assent would not become law, said Dave Guénette, director of the Observatory for Research on Constitutional Issues at the Université de Sherbrooke.
'Ready for a battle'
Pressed again on Wednesday about the legal requirements, St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down, suggesting he is ready for a jurisdictional battle with the federal government.

"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters, noting that Quebec never consented to the 1982 repatriation of the Constitution.
The PQ's unscripted announcement on Tuesday was sparked by a Le Devoir report revealing that a trip to Scandinavia and Greenland by Governor General Mary Simon cost taxpayers more than $700,000.
St-Pierre Plamondon estimated that Canada spends between $50 million and $60 million annually on the monarchy nationwide.
That estimate is consistent with one made by the Monarchist League of Canada.

Based on Quebec's proportion of the national population, St-Pierre Plamondon said Quebecers send $12 million to $15 million a year to Ottawa to support the Crown — funds he noted Quebec cannot stop paying unless the province becomes independent.

items: A victory for the separatist PQ would present political test for Carney
Indigenous leaders remind Quebec: you can't legally separate without our say

blocks.text: If elected, St-Pierre Plamondon also said his government would break with parliamentary tradition by asking the lieutenant-governor not to attend the opening address of the new legislative session.
The PQ has pushed constitutional boundaries regarding the monarchy before.
In 2022, under intense pressure from the PQ, the National Assembly unanimously passed a bill ending the requirement for elected members to swear an oath to the King before taking their seats.

That change is the subject of a legal challenge in Quebec Superior Court. The plaintiffs in that case argue the provincial government overstepped its jurisdiction, and that removing the oath also required the unanimous consent of Parliament and the provinces. A ruling has yet to be issued.
Referendum talk dominates Quebec election campaign, but what about Indigenous sovereignty?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Benjamin Shingler is a reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at CTV, The Canadian Press and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. He can be reached at benjamin.shingler@cbc.ca.
With files from Cathy Senay and Radio-Canada's La vérif

articles.title: GG marks 6th National Day for Truth and Reconciliation with plea for 'understanding the truth'

image.caption: The Survivors' Flag will be raised again on Parliament Hill in Ottawa to mark the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, with Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour among those in attendance. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
As Canadians mark the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour says it's important to face an "unsettling" past in order to build a better country.
'We cannot change the past, but we can choose how we move forward,' Louise Arbour says
This is Arbour's first time observing the day as Governor General. She was sworn in this summer, replacing Mary Simon, the first Indigenous person to serve in the role.

"Many Canadians, myself included, did not grow up knowing this history. Facing it can be painful and unsettling, but understanding the truth is essential to building a more just future," Arbour said in a statement Wednesday.
"We cannot change the past, but we can choose how we move forward."
Arbour said understanding Canada's historical truth begins with "empathy" for First Nations, Inuit and Métis.

"It continues through honest dialogue, ongoing learning and concrete action to address the inequities inherited from past wrongs. Together, we can build a country where these injustices are never repeated."

items: Almost 40K residential school records will be destroyed. Not all survivors think they should be

blocks.text: Arbour took part in the re-raising of the Survivors' Flag on Parliament Hill in Ottawa and delivered remarks to honour residential school survivors.
Prime Minister Mark Carney will be in Edmonton to mark the occasion and is set to speak at a commemorative event.
Children forced to leave families
Canada's residential schools operated from 1857 to 1996. Some 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to leave their families to attend the government or church-run institutions.
Decades after death, residential school student buried on First Nation
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's (TRC) exhaustive, years-long study of residential schools revealed the devastating impact they had on Indigenous people.

items: Watch 7 powerful Indigenous stories on CBC Gem for National Day of Truth and Reconciliation

blocks.text: The institutions were designed to assimilate Indigenous children into the dominant Euro-Canadian culture, causing deep intergenerational trauma and harm, the TRC found. They were characterized by widespread abuse and neglect, and led to as many as 6,000 deaths, mostly from malnutrition or disease.
Eleven years after the publication of the TRC report, only 15 of its 94 calls to action have been put into force.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title: Ontario trial into boy's death shows need to learn how to 'show up for an Indigenous child:' advocate
articles.summary: Halton Indigenous advocate Jody Harbour says a months-long murder trial in Milton, Ont., shone a light on "the continuing crisis of Indigenous child welfare in Ontario." The co-founder of…

image.caption: A observer wearing an orange shirt pin attends a reporter scrum outside the courthouse in Milton, Ont., on May 5, 2026. Becky Hamber, 46, and Brandy Cooney, 44, were found guilty in the first-degree murder of a 12-year-old boy in 2022 and of torturing his younger brother. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Halton Indigenous advocate Jody Harbour says a months-long murder trial in Milton, Ont., shone a light on "the continuing crisis of Indigenous child welfare in Ontario." The co-founder of Grandmother's Voice said change means ensuring front-line workers know how to support Indigenous people.
Trial of Brandy Cooney and Becky Hamber raised concerns about child welfare system
WARNING: This story details violence and child abuse.
For Halton Indigenous advocate Jody Harbour, a months-long murder trial in Milton, Ont., shone a light on "the continuing crisis of Indigenous child welfare in Ontario."
In July, two Burlington, Ont., women were sentenced to life in prison for the murder of an Indigenous boy they were trying to adopt, and for crimes against his younger brother, including assault.

Multiple observers have said the trial raised concerns about the child protection system and showcased systemic issues that need to be addressed immediately, including reducing the number of Indigenous children in care and working more closely with Indigenous groups and families to establish appropriate care.

At the July sentencing and other points during the trial, Indigenous community members came to Milton, Ont., to bear witness and support the boys' family. That included Harbour, co-founder of Oakville, Ont., Indigenous organization Grandmother's Voice.

items: Children's aid system faces heightened calls for change after Ontario couple's murder, torture convictions

blocks.text: Speaking to CBC Hamilton before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Harbour said that since the sentencing, she's spent hours scrolling through comments and messages written by people who say they've been harmed by the child welfare system.
For her, the case highlighted a need for people at children's aid societies to understand "Indigenous ways of knowing."
"Front-line responders, support workers, the people on the ground [need to] understand what it means to show up for an Indigenous child," she said.

The months-long trial in Milton, Ont., heard the older boy, L.L., died on Dec. 21, 2022, after he was found unresponsive and emaciated in the basement bedroom of the family home. Superior Court Justice Clayton Conlan convicted his prospective adoptive parents Brandy Cooney and Becky Hamber of his murder in May.

items: Ontario murder case highlights child welfare's systemic failures, say advocates

blocks.text: L.L. and his younger brother, J.L., entered the child protection system when the older boy was a toddler due to concerns over their home environment that weren't detailed during the trial. CBC is referring to the boys using initials due to a standard publication ban on their identities.

L.L. and J.L. were moved from Ottawa to live with Cooney and Hamber in Burlington in 2017, but remained wards of the Ottawa Children's Aid Society (CAS). The Halton CAS was in charge of supervising the family on a daily basis.

The trial heard Halton CAS received many reports from people concerned about how Hamber and Cooney were treating the boys, yet workers never did unannounced home visits, nor did they interview the boys without Cooney or Hamber present, as is required.
Both CAS agencies previously told CBC they completed reviews for the Cooney-Hamber case and made changes after L.L. died. They haven’t shared specifics about those changes.
Closing arguments start in case of Ontario boy allegedly killed by couple trying to adopt him
Halton CAS says it continues to 'engage' Indigenous communities

CBC Hamilton asked Halton CAS to confirm whether it has met or continues to meet with local Indigenous groups and community members about issues raised during that trial. CBC also asked the agency to comment on any specific steps it has taken to help its staff better support Indigenous families and children in their day-to-day work.

In an email, an agency spokesperson who did not provide their name said Halton CAS has "a long-standing commitment and practice of working in partnership with communities, partner organizations and service providers to support the safety and well-being of children, youth, and families."

CAS said it "continues to engage with Indigenous community leaders, representatives, and service providers to strengthen partnerships and enhance supports for Indigenous children, youth, and families.

"We have also expanded Indigenous-focused training and practice supports for staff, with an emphasis on culturally-responsive, relationship-based, and trauma-informed approaches that inform our day-to-day work," the email said.

Harbour identifies as an urban Indigenous person with Cayuga and Ojibwa roots. She said the Haudenosaunee grandmothers and Anishinabek elders that guide the work of her organization are passionate about ensuring systems including children's aid societies do the the work they need to keep Indigenous kids safe.
Since L.L.'s death, Harbour said her organization has been in touch with Halton CAS and other local front-line organizations in order to "make change in [his] name."
She said one of those efforts is an ongoing program to provide front-line workers with "cultural trauma training," so they can better support urban Indigenous people.

Harbour said she believes that too often, frontline workers lack the tools they need to do so. She added it's also important for organizations to support any Indigenous workers brought in to educate, so they don't burnout from dealing with trauma.
Making change is “not about pointing fingers because those are human beings that work within CAS," Harbour said. "Reconciliation is saying we want to reconcile. We want to work together."
National Day for Truth and Reconciliation 2026 | CBC News Special

In March, Ottawa-based First Nations child advocate Cindy Blackstock told CBC News the trial brought home the need to implement the first five calls to action from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada. According to CBC tracker Beyond 94, none of those recommendations focused on the child-welfare system has been completed.
Sherry Saevil, a member of Mistawasis First Nation and a Halton resident shared similar thoughts.
Saevil was part of the Indigenous collective, Circle of Beads, that came together outside the Halton Children’s Aid Society in 2024 to raise awareness about the case.
In May, Saevil said she hopes there'll be an overhaul of the child welfare system and an inquest that examines the role of the Children's Aid Society agencies in this case.
The five TRC recommendations on child welfare are:

items: Reduce the number of Indigenous children in care.
Publish annual reports on the number of Indigenous children in care.
Implement Jordan's Principle.
Enact child welfare legislation that establishes national standards for Indigenous child apprehension and custody cases.
Develop culturally appropriate parenting programs for Indigenous families.

blocks.text: Blackstock said governments need to do more to make changes that are structural and significant or there will be more deaths.
“The biggest price is paid by children," she said, "who pay with their lives and their childhood."

If you’re affected by this report, you can look for mental health support through resources in your province or territory . If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Chandler is a CBC News reporter in Hamilton. He covers stories of all kinds from places including picket lines, court rooms, council meetings and research labs. Justin has a special interest in how public policy affects people, and loves a quirky human-interest story. Before CBC Hamilton, he worked for TVO and on a variety of CBC teams and programs. He co-hosted Radio Free Krypton on Met Radio.
